articles.title: Vietnam just got zero tariffs in Europe. Latin American exporters should be worried. - Latin Times
articles.summary: Vietnam just got zero tariffs in Europe. Latin American exporters should be worried.  Latin Times
articles.full_text:
Vietnam did not wait for Latin America to catch up.
While South American and Mexican exporters were still absorbing the ripple effects of their own hard-won market openings, Hanoi moved — completing a sweeping trade pact with Europe's second commercial bloc one day after the rest of the world's attention was focused elsewhere. The consequences for Latin American manufacturers are not theoretical; they are structural, and they are already in motion.
A 14-Year Deal With Immediate Market Consequences
Vietnam and the European Free Trade Association formally concluded a comprehensive free trade agreement on October 18, 2026, in Hanoi, after fourteen years and 21 rounds of negotiations that began in 2012 and were interrupted for years before resuming in 2025. The ceremony brought together Lê Mạnh Hùng, Vietnam's Minister of Industry and Trade, who signed the document on Hanoi's behalf, alongside the heads of government of Norway, Switzerland, Iceland, and Liechtenstein.
President and General Secretary Tô Lâm — Vietnam's top leader, holding the country's two most powerful positions simultaneously — attended the Hanoi ceremony in person, a signal that this was not a routine trade formality but a presidential-level strategic commitment.
The scope of the agreement is broad: it addresses trade in goods and services, rules of origin, intellectual property rights, government procurement, investment, sanitary measures, and sustainable development. But it is the tariff architecture that carries the most immediate competitive weight.
Under the deal, EFTA members immediately liberalize more than 90% of tariff lines, representing 99.5% of Vietnam's current exports to the bloc. Covered products include textiles and garments, footwear, seafood, computers and electronic components, and machinery and equipment. Vietnamese agricultural goods — including rice, honey, and fruit — also receive tariff reductions. Selected European products such as cheese and chocolate will gain duty-free access to the Vietnamese market, but only after a transition period of up to 16 years.
The EFTA Prize: A $630 Billion Market With Room to Grow
The commercial opportunity at stake is considerable. EFTA's annual import turnover runs to roughly $630 billion, and Vietnamese goods currently account for just 0.65% of that figure. Bilateral trade between EFTA and Vietnam totaled €4.8 billion in 2025, with Vietnam running a €2.5 billion surplus — a gap that has widened sharply compared with a decade earlier.
For Colombian garment producers, Brazilian footwear exporters, and Mexican electronics assemblers competing for shelf space in Zurich or Oslo, the arithmetic is straightforward: their Vietnamese rivals now pay zero import duties, while Latin American goods still face standard EFTA tariff rates. The competitive floor has shifted, and there is no reversal mechanism built into the agreement.
The Mercosur Flank: Vietnam Takes the Competition South
The EFTA pact drew the headlines, but a simultaneous diplomatic push may ultimately prove more consequential for the region. Vietnam is negotiating directly with South America's largest economic bloc — not just for market access in Europe, but for preferential access to Mercosur's domestic markets themselves.
The first round of negotiations for the Vietnam–Mercosur Preferential Trade Agreement concluded on August 28, 2026, after five days of technical sessions in Buenos Aires, with Argentina coordinating the bloc's side. The framing on both ends was optimistic: Argentine officials highlighted that bilateral trade had doubled over the past decade, growing from approximately $6.6 billion in 2015 to more than $12 billion in 2025, without any preferential framework in place.
If a preferential deal is reached, the implications for Brazilian and Argentine manufacturers extend beyond export competition in third markets. Vietnamese electronics — which generated nearly $165 billion in export revenue in 2025 — would gain improved access to the Brazilian and Argentine consumer market, the very domestic revenue base that regional producers depend on when global export conditions tighten.
Latin American Textiles and Electronics Face a Structural Squeeze
For the textile sector on both continents, the combined effect of Vietnam's European trade moves represents a pincer movement.
Brazil's textile and apparel industry counts 25,700 businesses employing approximately 1.3 million workers and generating $40.9 billion in annual revenue. The sector had cautiously welcomed the EU–Mercosur agreement — signed in Asunción on January 17, 2026 — as a pathway to expanded European market access. Industry associations representing Brazilian manufacturers (ABIT), their Argentine counterparts (FITA), and Europe's own textile lobby (EURATEX) issued a joint statement in February calling the deal "essential" for competitiveness on both sides of the Atlantic.
Vietnam's EFTA deal partially neutralizes that advantage. European buyers who might have shifted sourcing toward Mercosur suppliers under the new EU framework now have an equally competitive Vietnamese alternative — one that operates under zero tariffs across both EU and EFTA channels simultaneously.
The overlap in export categories is not coincidental. Vietnam's textile and garment industry posted $46 billion in exports in 2025 and has set a $50 billion target for 2026, driven by the same European and American buyers that Latin American producers compete for. Vietnam is already the world's second-largest garment exporter. The EFTA deal adds one more preferential lane to a network that already covers most of its major trading partners.
Hanoi's Export Pivot and the U.S. Tariff Pressure
The aggressive pace of trade diversification is not a coincidence of timing. Vietnam has been under sustained pressure to reduce its dependence on the U.S. market, which absorbs roughly 30% of Vietnam's total exports. That reliance became a structural liability after Washington imposed reciprocal tariffs that left Vietnamese textile and garment exports facing a 12.5% U.S. import duty — 2.5 percentage points above the 10% rate applied to some regional competitors — according to the Vietnam Textile and Apparel Association.
Vietnam's response has been systematic: conclude the EFTA deal, push for EU-market access under the existing EU–Vietnam FTA (in force since 2020), and now open negotiations with Mercosur. Taken together, the strategy is to spread export volume across so many preferential lanes that no single market disruption — however large — can destabilize the country's export-driven growth model.
What Latin American Trade Ministries Must Reckon With Now
The Vietnam–Mercosur PTA remains at an early stage, and the EFTA deal must pass parliamentary ratification in each member country before entering full force. But direction matters as much as timeline in trade policy, and the direction here is unambiguous.
Vietnam is no longer simply an Asian competitor in Asian-facing supply chains. It is now an active rival in European markets — and a prospective entrant to South American domestic ones. For trade ministries from Bogotá to São Paulo, the question is no longer whether to respond; it is how fast a coordinated response can be assembled, and whether the advantages secured under the EU–Mercosur agreement will be enough to offset what Hanoi has just put in place.

articles.title: Representative Tran Quoc Tuan: Addressing import-export shortcomings, controlling inflation, and reducing growth pressure on businesses. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Representative Tran Quoc Tuan: Addressing import-export shortcomings, controlling inflation, and reducing growth pressure on businesses.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On October 18, 2026, speaking at the group discussion session on the socio -economic situation in 2026 and orientation for 2027, delegate Tran Quoc Tuan, member of the Standing Committee of the Provincial Party Committee and Director of the Department of Industry and Trade of Vinh Long province, contributed many practical and insightful opinions from the perspective of managing the industry and trade sector and supporting businesses.
 Delegates pointed out shortcomings in the structure of the trade deficit, the health of businesses, and inflationary pressures, while also recommending that the Government remove legal bottlenecks and pay attention to the welfare of officials and civil servants in the face of significant economic growth pressures. 
|  | 
| Delegate Tran Quoc Tuan, member of the Standing Committee of the Provincial Party Committee and Director of the Department of Industry and Trade of Vinh Long province, delivered a speech at the group meeting on the morning of October 18th. | 
 Shortcomings in the import structure and dependence on foreign raw materials.
 Analyzing the data for the first nine months of the year, delegate Tran Quoc Tuan pointed out a paradox: exports increased by 24.5%, but imports increased by as much as 36.7%, resulting in a trade deficit of $19.42 billion. Of this, the FDI sector had a trade surplus of $14 billion, while domestic enterprises had a trade deficit of $33.42 billion; over 94% of imported goods were production materials.
 The delegate cited the pharmaceutical industry, which currently imports over 90% of its raw materials from India and China. This excessive reliance on foreign inputs makes domestic production vulnerable to fluctuations in transportation costs, exchange rates, and supply chain disruptions, while also putting pressure on the balance of payments and inflation. The delegate suggested that the government should direct the detailed separation of import data (what goods, which industries they serve, and how much domestic added value they create) to develop policies for supporting industries and strengthen linkages between FDI enterprises and Vietnamese businesses, instead of mechanically aiming to reduce imports, which could lead to raw material shortages.
 Assessing the health of businesses and pressures in the retail sector.
 Expressing concern over the figure of 172,000 businesses withdrawing from the market in the first nine months (while only 149,700 new businesses were established), the delegate noted that the pressure is mainly concentrated in small businesses and the service, wholesale, and retail sectors (67,300 businesses leaving the market). The withdrawal of businesses leads to difficulties in capital, employment, and input services. The delegate suggested that, in addition to encouraging the establishment of new businesses, the Government should assess the causes by industry and scale to focus on removing difficulties related to working capital, input costs, and administrative procedures, helping businesses maintain their vitality. 
|  | 
| A view of the National Assembly delegates from Vinh Long and Lao Cai provinces participating in discussion session number 15. | 
 Controlling inflation and interest rate and credit pressures.
 On a macroeconomic level, delegates expressed concern that the CPI for the first nine months increased by 4.52% (close to the target of 4.5%), with housing, electricity, water, and construction material prices rising by as much as 6.68%, and transportation by 6.06%. While total retail sales increased by 13.4% at current prices, the actual increase was only nearly 8% after excluding inflation, indicating that prices are eroding consumer purchasing power and driving up business costs.
 Furthermore, with the average new lending interest rate at 9.12% per year and the credit-to-GDP ratio reaching 155%, the economy is heavily dependent on credit. The representative requested that the Government clarify the structure of credit allocated to different sectors (public investment, real estate, manufacturing, agriculture ) in order to develop monetary policies that reduce actual borrowing costs for businesses.
 Removing legal bottlenecks and reducing compliance costs for local authorities.
 Delegates pointed out that many of the Central Committee's policies and resolutions are very decisive, but their practical implementation still faces obstacles at the ministerial and sectoral levels. For example, in Vinh Long, the potential for renewable energy with approximately 4,600 MW of wind power is being hampered by the lack of investment approval under Resolution 254 due to land and sea boundary issues, requiring the locality to seek opinions from the Provincial Party Standing Committee and the Executive Committee. Similarly, there are obstacles in Decree 320 regarding the conversion of corporate income tax from 17% to 10%, which businesses cannot pay due to procedural bottlenecks at the tax authorities. Delegates emphasized that if these bottlenecks are genuinely removed, private resources will be strongly unlocked for growth.
 High growth, significant pressure on grassroots officials, and proposals for salary reform.
 Sharing his thoughts on the pressures of governance, delegate Tran Quoc Tuan stated that the team of officials and civil servants (especially at the grassroots level) are working intensely day and night, including holidays, to achieve double-digit growth targets. For example, in Vinh Long, achieving a growth target of 17.25% in the fourth quarter of 2026, after reaching only 7.32% in the first nine months, is an unprecedented level, placing immense pressure on the administrative apparatus.
 Based on that reality, delegates proposed that the Government should expedite the implementation of salary reform in accordance with Resolution 27 to ensure adequate remuneration and income to compensate for labor, create motivation for officials and civil servants to work with peace of mind and successfully complete their tasks.

articles.title: ASEAN should focus on building up regional power grid, climate finance, and resilience: Grace Fu - Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.summary: ASEAN should focus on building up regional power grid, climate finance, and resilience: Grace Fu  Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB)
articles.full_text:
Speaking at an event where a survey of Southeast Asian perceptions on climate change was released, she said that Singapore will, during its chairmanship of ASEAN in 2027, prioritise practical cooperation on these issues.
The Southeast Asia Climate Outlook Survey 2026 is a biennial survey that aims to gauge regional attitudes towards climate change.
In its sixth edition, the survey was released by the Climate Change in Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and the Lee Kuan Yew Centre for Innovative Cities at the Singapore University of Technology and Design.
The survey found that the top two concerns faced by people in Southeast Asia were unemployment and economic recession, as well as climate change and extreme weather events.
This comes at a time when the closure of the Strait of Hormuz is sending shockwaves through global energy markets, Fu said.
“Southeast Asia has not been spared. For a region heavily reliant on imported energy, higher fuel prices ripple quickly through everyday life,” she said.
Businesses face rising costs and growing uncertainty, putting jobs and livelihoods at stake. Households also have to grapple with higher electricity bills, while some supermarkets lack food because transportation and logistical support are affected.
At the same time, the region must also respond to impacts already being felt. For example, recent heavy rain in Thailand has led to floods in areas including Bangkok and reportedly affected more than 2.6 million people.
Fu noted that the energy crisis is a good reason for the transition to renewable energy, and that pausing this shift might be the wrong response.
She noted that the rapid deployment of solar energy in countries such as China and Pakistan has reduced their exposure to imported fossil fuels, therefore restricting exposure to volatile fuel prices.

articles.full_text:
Malaysia’s haze frustration boils over school closures as calls grow to hold polluters to account
AI generated
KUALA LUMPUR/JOHOR BAHRU – Every day this week, 45-year-old executive Alisha Chan has been reaching for her phone to check pollution readings and school announcements to find out whether her children will be going to school the next day – and whether she needs to arrange childcare around her full-time job.
With two school-going children aged 17 and seven, she faces the possibility of disruptions to family routines and work when haze from fires in Indonesia forces schools to close.
“We parents are living in fear, constantly checking for updates on school closures. It feels like a time bomb,” she told The Straits Times on Oct 14.
“Today, while we were preparing for our children to stay home because of the school closures, the Education Ministry suddenly announced that schools would be open as usual tomorrow.
“We can’t plan things in advance and have to make arrangements at the last minute, which is stressful for a full-time working mother. I feel exhausted and have a headache from all these last-minute arrangements as we are not employees who can work from home every day.”
The frustration has also spilt into online education support groups, with parents unhappy over the issue of school closures.
Indonesia is experiencing an unusually severe fire season, with prolonged heat and dryness exacerbated by a very strong El Nino. Fires are burning large areas of Sumatra and Kalimantan, blanketing the region in haze.
After decades of recurring episodes, Malaysians are growing increasingly frustrated – not just at the disruption, but at the apparent failure of national and regional authorities to hold polluters to account and prevent the crisis from recurring.
The recent school closures in some states have added to parents’ frustration, with last-minute announcements making childcare arrangements difficult for working families.
The shifting announcements have become one immediate source of that frustration.
School closures leave parents scrambling
K. Rizal, whose 10-year-old child attends school in Kuala Lumpur, said school closures depend on readings from designated air-quality monitoring stations, which may not reflect conditions in every neighbourhood.
“I can see the haze, but because the reading at the monitoring station is fine, we have to pretend like it’s okay and go to school,” she told ST, calling for schools to have more flexibility to decide when to close.
“We can see the difference between a clear day and a heavily hazy day. Some of us also experience eye irritation, throat discomfort or difficulty breathing. If healthy adults already feel uncomfortable, naturally we worry about our children,” Ameirul Azraie Mustadza, a father of five and chairman of a parent-teacher association, told ST.
“Parents need confidence that the system can respond to the conditions their children are experiencing. Clear explanations, timely communication and responsive action are essential to building that confidence,” he added.
On Oct 7, some 20 protesters from Greenpeace Malaysia and a coalition of environmental and civil society groups marched to Parliament, demanding stronger laws to hold companies accountable for environmental damage linked to fires in Indonesia.
“Enforcement is an issue... At the end of the day, it’s the governments that approve the operating licences and financial institutions that oversee financing for these companies,” Adam Azlan, a global strategic campaigner for international environmental organisation Greenpeace, told ST.
The campaigners want governments to investigate links between fires and corporate operations, make evidence public and enforce environmental rules, alongside a Clean Air Act to hold Malaysian businesses accountable for haze pollution caused by their overseas operations.
While these may take time, for families, the consequences of the haze are immediate.
School closures can protect children from unhealthy air, but announcements made late in the afternoon leave parents scrambling to arrange childcare, rearrange work schedules and supervise home-based online learning instead.
The week-long school closures in Johor announced on Oct 10 amid worsening haze conditions have given parents there greater certainty, but still complicate childcare arrangements, particularly for those who work across the Causeway in Singapore.
Truck driver Shahruddin Haeal Helmy Mohd Noh, 39, who lives in Iskandar Puteri, Johor, works in Singapore, as does his wife. They have had to take their two children to their grandparents’ home amid the school closures.
“The school closures are definitely a challenge because we need to find caregiving arrangements for our children while my wife and I are at work in Singapore,” he said, adding that unpredictable work schedules and cross-border traffic make planning difficult.
Fariza Mohd, an assistant manager at a private after-school care centre in Pasir Gudang, Johor, said staff were overwhelmed as more working parents turned to daycare during school closures.
“Usually we have 40 students split into two sessions, morning and afternoon, but now we have 25 to 30 children staying for the entire day,” she said. With home-based learning, all three staff members must also help supervise lessons for the children.
Changing rules add to confusion
The uncertainty has been compounded by changing closure thresholds and differences in local air-quality readings.
On Oct 14, Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek reinstated the threshold for school closures at Air Pollutant Index (API) readings above 200, reversing temporary rules introduced on Oct 8 that required closures when readings exceeded 180, or 150 for three consecutive days.
API readings ranging from zero and 50 indicate good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, and 201 to 300 very unhealthy, while readings above 300 are categorised as hazardous.
Fadhlina ruled out blanket closures announced days in advance, citing rapidly changing air quality.
“Children’s safety and health remain our priority. However, every school day also holds significant value for their development and learning,” she said in a Facebook post on Oct 14.
Parents who remain concerned about their children’s health and safety may keep them at home, she said.
That post attracted around 4,000 comments, with some criticising the Education Ministry’s apparent lack of consistent policies and contingency plans.
The Melaka Action Group for Parents in Education urged the authorities to clarify school-closure guidelines and announce closures earlier, preferably by noon the previous day, to give parents, teachers and school transport operators time to prepare.
“This is not about criticising the authorities for taking precautionary measures. Rather, it is about ensuring that decisions affecting students, teachers and thousands of families are transparent, consistent and properly communicated,” its chairman Mak Chee Kin was quoted as saying by the Free Malaysia Today news website on Oct 14.
The debate over closures is also raising questions about what happens to children when they are told to learn from home.
Online learning is no easy fix
The concerns extend beyond whether classrooms are open.
For some families, switching to online classes is no easy solution, particularly if children lack devices, reliable internet connections or support at home.
“Home-based learning should not become a mere formality. Schools must consider whether students have access to devices, internet connectivity and appropriate learning support, particularly those from disadvantaged households,” education watchdog Parent Action Group for Education’s chairman Noor Azimah Abdul Rahim told ST.
Malaysian frustration has also stemmed from Jakarta’s handling of the crisis, including its initial hesitation over foreign assistance and remarks by an Indonesian official that drew criticism online.
Democratic Action Party MP Lim Guan Eng said in Parliament on Oct 15 that Malaysia must stop taking a lax approach to the recurring haze crisis, urging Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and Indonesia to establish a permanent ASEAN task force with year-round firefighting personnel.
“If Indonesia continues to reject the ASEAN haze task force on grounds of national sovereignty, Malaysia has no choice but to pursue legal action to seek compensation.”
The Malaysian-Indonesia Journalists’ Friendship Association has also called for stronger enforcement against open burning, closer bilateral cooperation and more effective ASEAN action.
“Cross-border haze can no longer be seen as a seasonal problem without an effective long-term solution,” said its acting president, Ahmad Zaini Kamaruzzaman, in an Oct 12 statement.
Remarks by an Indonesian official that the country supplies oxygen to Singapore and Malaysia drew criticism online.
On Oct 10, Syahganda Nainggolan, head of Indonesia’s Government Communications Agency, defended the country against criticism over transboundary haze, saying: “We’re not just sending over the haze. When there’s no haze, we send oxygen. The oxygen in Singapore and Malaysia comes from our forests, right?”
Threads user veronicazo said: “Someone please inform the Ministry of Education. We have an entire primary school science syllabus to amend.”

articles.title: With record FDI growth, where do Vietnamese businesses stand in the supply chain? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: With record FDI growth, where do Vietnamese businesses stand in the supply chain?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Vietnam continues to be a positive destination for foreign direct investment (FDI). A notable sign is the increasing number of domestic businesses participating in the supply chains of foreign companies. However, the level of integration remains an area for improvement.
Vietnamese businesses are more confident when participating in supply chains.
At the recent 2026 Export Forum, a leader in charge of Samsung Vietnam's Purchasing Center stated that the corporation is seeking Vietnamese suppliers that meet new standards regarding consistent quality, technological capabilities, data-driven operations, and sustainable development. Competitive pricing is no longer the sole factor in partner selection.
Samsung is also preparing to expand its support for Vietnam's supporting industries from Bac Ninh and Ho Chi Minh City to key industrial areas such as Phu Tho, Hai Phong, and Thai Nguyen. This will give many local businesses the opportunity to access cooperation programs, improve their production capacity, and meet the requirements of major buyers.
Conversely, domestic businesses are also striving to participate in the supply network for foreign companies. Mr. Do Phuoc Tong, Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City Mechanical and Electrical Business Association, announced that his company has approached and supplied 1-2 FDI companies in Vietnam during this year's new wave of investment. Although the orders are still modest, this signals that opportunities remain wide open for well-prepared and experienced companies participating in the supply chain.
"We have been supplying components and spare parts for assembling equipment and machinery for about 10 FDI enterprises in the form of on-site export within the industrial park for many years. Sales from this activity have increased by about 10-20%," Mr. Tong said, noting that the level of participation of domestic enterprises in the FDI supply chain is increasing. They are also more confident and proactive, especially as FDI corporations that have invested in Vietnam for many years continue to expand production and seek domestic suppliers.
You may also like
In Northern Vietnam, An Trung Industries, part of the An Phat ecosystem, became a Tier 2 supplier for Samsung in 2019 through Elentec Vietnam Co., Ltd., and subsequently a Tier 1 supplier for Brother Vietnam. Currently, the company manufactures components for corporations such as Samsung, Foxconn, Panasonic, and Brother Vietnam. To increase production capacity, An Trung Industries is investing over VND 1.15 trillion in building a high-tech plastic mold and component manufacturing plant in An Phat 1 Industrial Park, with an expected capacity of 15,500 tons of products and 340 mold sets per year. Meanwhile, Manh Toan Plastic Co., Ltd., specializing in the processing and manufacturing of high-end technical and household plastic products for export, currently supplies approximately 70% of its products to FDI enterprises from China and South Korea .
On the other hand, despite positive signs, it cannot be denied that Vietnamese businesses' participation in the supply chains of foreign companies remains modest. According to Mr. Do Phuoc Tong, becoming a supplier is not simple. Businesses must invest in machinery, production systems, and continuously upgrade their capabilities. Quality requirements are increasingly stringent, and certifications and standards such as ISO must be regularly updated. Therefore, although opportunities are increasing, meeting all the conditions of FDI corporations remains a significant challenge.
A major challenge is competition from foreign businesses, especially Chinese businesses that are relocating to Vietnam. These businesses have advantages in financial resources, experience, long-standing partner networks, and an established manufacturing ecosystem. Meanwhile, Vietnamese businesses are limited in capital and supporting industrial capacity, making it difficult for them to compete.
Mr. Tong noted the need to distinguish between increasing domestic purchases in Vietnam and developing purely Vietnamese businesses to participate in the supply chain. Goods purchased in Vietnam may be produced by Vietnamese businesses or foreign-invested businesses in Vietnam. Therefore, an increase in the proportion of domestic purchases does not necessarily mean that the capacity of domestic businesses will improve accordingly. Products manufactured in Vietnam also do not mean that Vietnamese businesses master the technology and create core value. Therefore, in addition to attracting FDI, more breakthrough policies are needed to enhance the capacity of domestic businesses, especially in terms of capital, technology, and the ability to meet the standards of global corporations.
Maintaining the attractiveness of FDI and strengthening the internal capacity of Vietnamese businesses.
In fact, the need to increase the localization rate and develop Vietnamese suppliers has been more clearly stated in Notice No. 481 dated September 14, 2026, from the Government Office. The concluding statement of Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc at a meeting with the Vietnam Electronics Business Association and several large electronics import-export businesses pointed out that the percentage of Vietnamese businesses participating in production and supply chains remains low. The electronics industry still heavily relies on foreign sources of components, raw materials, and technology, while domestic added value remains limited.
Economist Pham Chi Lan recommends that Vietnam should continue to maintain its attractiveness to FDI flows, but cannot become dependent on this sector and must strengthen the domestic business sector. The increasing contribution of the FDI sector to total export turnover shows the important role of this capital flow in the economy, but also indicates the need to strengthen the domestic sector.
The challenge is not just attracting more FDI, but also creating conditions for Vietnamese businesses to improve their production capacity, master technology, and become genuine partners of multinational corporations. Only when domestic capacity is improved can FDI flows have a greater ripple effect, helping Vietnamese businesses participate more deeply in the global value chain.
You may also like
Economist Pham Chi Lan
Another issue, according to Ms. Pham Chi Lan, is that the majority of capital flows still come from Asian countries such as Singapore, South Korea, and Japan, while the proportion from the European Union, Canada, and other partners remains modest.
Expert Pham Chi Lan emphasized that in the coming period, FDI policy needs to be adjusted to increase the requirement for linkages with domestic businesses. The 100% foreign-owned investment model, which was essential during Vietnam's opening-up period, should not be applied indiscriminately anymore. Instead, more focus should be placed on creating linkages, transferring capabilities, and helping domestic businesses participate more deeply in supply chains. Along with adjusting FDI policy, Vietnam needs a clear strategy to encourage the domestic private sector, especially large enterprises, to invest more heavily in new industries and technologies.
"The challenge is not just attracting more FDI, but also creating conditions for Vietnamese businesses to improve their production capacity, master technology, and become genuine partners of multinational corporations. Only when domestic capacity is improved can FDI flows create a greater ripple effect, helping Vietnamese businesses participate more deeply in the global value chain," said economist Pham Chi Lan.
According to the Department of Industry (Ministry of Industry and Trade), the localization rate and the level of participation in global value chains of Vietnamese supporting industrial enterprises are still low. Specifically, the localization rate in key industries such as electronics is only about 35%, textiles and footwear about 45-55%, mechanical engineering about 25-30%, and passenger cars about 15-20%..., all much lower than in other countries in the region.

articles.title: Pressure to manage capital costs and fluctuations in construction material prices are impacting growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Pressure to manage capital costs and fluctuations in construction material prices are impacting growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Barriers such as interest rate differentials, a credit-to-GDP ratio of 155%, and fluctuating commodity prices are posing challenges to long-term growth targets.
During the socio -economic discussion session in the National Assembly, delegates focused on analyzing bottlenecks in financial resources and input material costs. Data presented showed that inflationary pressures, capital costs, and construction material prices are creating significant obstacles to achieving a GDP growth target of 10% or more by 2027.
Capital flow structure and the challenge of sustainable interest rate reduction.
Representative To Huy Vu ( Hanoi delegation) noted that despite improvements in the national credit rating and an upgrade in the stock market, macroeconomic pressures remain. The average consumer price index (CPI) for the first nine months increased by 4.52%, approaching the target of approximately 4.5% for 2027. Credit growth reached about 11.59%, while the rate of capital mobilization only reached 8.83%.
Notably, the credit-to-GDP ratio has reached approximately 155%, indicating that the size of bank credit is currently 1.5 times GDP. Nearly 80% of mobilized capital has a maturity of less than 12 months, creating a mismatch in maturities, as the demand for development investment is primarily medium and long-term. Furthermore, the disbursement of public investment remains slow, and the real estate market is facing liquidity difficulties.
To address the challenge of reducing capital costs without risking inflation, delegates proposed restructuring capital channels instead of relying solely on commercial banks competing by reducing profit margins. Key solutions include:
You may also like
Increase the charter capital of state-owned commercial banks to enhance their leading role in the market.
Control liquidity risk and monitor credit growth at weak financial institutions.
Leverage public debt capacity through the issuance of government and local government bonds, while expanding ODA funding and mobilizing international capital.
Promoting the equitization of state-owned enterprises, developing the stock and corporate bond markets, and public-private partnerships (PPP).
Extend or phase out land-related financial obligations for production and social housing projects, combined with timely tax refunds and construction capital payments.
Pressure from price discrepancies in building materials and the supply of sand for leveling.
Regarding infrastructure investment, delegate Nguyen Khanh Vu (Quang Tri delegation) reflected on the shortage of supply affecting the progress of many projects. Citing data from the Ministry of Construction released on October 15th, the nationwide demand for leveling sand reached over 600 million m³, while the actual supply capacity only reached 394.5 million m³, a shortfall of over 200 million m³.
In Quang Tri province, despite having 224 quarry areas for construction stone and fill soil with a projected resource of over 1.28 billion cubic meters, construction sites still face material shortages. Price fluctuations have seen significant adjustments: the price of fine sand at some quarries has increased from 42% to over 147%, while the price of construction stone has increased by an average of 12–47%.
Representatives pointed out the inadequacy where actual transaction prices are higher than the inter-departmental prices, but sellers only issue invoices based on the published prices. As a result, construction companies have to cover the difference in costs themselves, and cannot deduct corporate income tax due to the lack of valid invoices. This leads to the paradox where construction companies incur losses in reality, but their accounting records still show profits and they have to pay taxes.
To address this issue, the proposed recommendations are that regulatory agencies should balance the supply and demand of materials in each region, linked to the list of public projects in 2027; ensure transparency in the licensing process; and increase mining capacity. Simultaneously, the tax authorities should coordinate with the Department of Construction to compare actual selling prices with electronic invoices to accurately reflect market prices in construction contracts.

| In the first eight months of 2026, shrimp exports reached US$3.29 billion, an increase of 12.3% and accounting for approximately 41% of total seafood export turnover. (Source: VASEP) | 
 According to the Vietnam Association of Seafood Processing and Export (VASEP), in the first eight months of 2026, shrimp exports reached US$3.29 billion, an increase of 12.3% and accounting for approximately 41% of total seafood export turnover. China was the main driving force with US$1.13 billion, an increase of 37.6%.
 This is seen as an important opportunity for businesses to capitalize on during the peak year-end period, especially since consumer demand in Asian markets typically increases before holidays and Tet (Lunar New Year). In addition, the need for importers to replenish their inventory after a period of cautious order placement could also provide further impetus for exports.
 However, the US market is posing significant challenges for Vietnamese shrimp. Shrimp exports to this market have decreased quite sharply recently. The Article 301 tariff is at 12.5%, higher than the 10% of some competitors, creating a price disadvantage. Meanwhile, the final results of the anti-dumping duty review, expected to be announced at the end of September, will directly impact orders in the fourth quarter.
 According to Ms. Le Hang, Deputy General Secretary of VASEP, the results of anti-dumping duties and Article 301 duties will influence orders from the US, offer prices, and market redirection speed. If the duty rates remain high, the flow of goods may continue to shift to Asia, putting further pressure on selling prices.
 Nevertheless, businesses still see opportunities in the US for highly processed, high-value-added products.
 According to Le Van Quang, General Director of Minh Phu Seafood Group Joint Stock Company, the US has surpassed Japan to become the company's largest market. Although Vietnamese shrimp is subject to an additional 12.5% tariff in the US, the difference compared to shrimp from India and Ecuador is not large enough to significantly reduce the competitiveness of value-added products.
 Increased demand is also driving businesses to expand their processing capacity. Minh Phu is accelerating automation, aiming for 70-80% automation in its production operations.
 Mr. Le Van Quang stated that even with all three factories operating at maximum capacity, the company still cannot meet all demand and may consider investing in additional factories if the market continues to grow.
 In addition, the frequent labor shortage has also contributed to Minh Phu's accelerated modernization and automation efforts. According to the company, robots can perform the workload equivalent to approximately three workers and operate continuously for three shifts.
 At the older factories, equipment will be replaced gradually. The Minh Phu Khanh An seafood processing plant in Ca Mau, in particular, has a designed capacity of 35,000 tons of products per year and has invested in a higher level of automation and robotics.
 One advantage of Vietnamese shrimp is its certified production system. Barbara Janker, Director of Trade for Europe and Asia-Pacific (APAC) at the Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC), stated that Vietnam is currently the world's third-largest producer of ASC-certified shrimp by volume. This is an advantage as demand for certified shrimp in Europe continues to grow.
 Besides shrimp, pangasius is seeing opportunities to expand its market as exports to the US decrease, while there is still room for growth in China, the EU, and the Middle East. In the EU, the shortage of natural whitefish supply and high cod prices create further room for Vietnamese pangasius.
 Another emerging trend attracting attention is tilapia. The gradual appearance of Vietnamese tilapia in sushi and sashimi dishes shows that this product can shift from competing on price to deeper processing and value-added segments. In particular, brackish water tilapia can create its own unique identity if quality control and management throughout the entire production chain are well-managed.
 According to VASEP, exceeding the $12 billion mark in seafood exports by 2026 remains feasible if Chinese demand is maintained and peak season orders are not disrupted. However, growth in the fourth quarter will be differentiated: shrimp may experience slower growth due to tariff pressure in the US; pangasius will rely more heavily on markets outside the US; while squid, octopus, crabs, and some mollusk groups could become bright spots.

articles.title: Banks cut interest rates: Sharing the pressure to support stock prices and profits. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Banks cut interest rates: Sharing the pressure to support stock prices and profits.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Banks must immediately reduce deposit interest rates by at least 0.5% per year and lending interest rates by 1.5-2% per year. This move aims to support businesses and boost economic growth, but it also raises questions about profitability and asset quality for the banking sector.
Many bank stocks fell in the trading session on October 19th, amid the State Bank of Vietnam's (SBV) directive for credit institutions to immediately reduce deposit and lending interest rates to support the economy and stabilize the monetary market.
At the close of trading, ACB shares fell 350 dong to 20,250 dong/share; BIDV (BID) fell 300 dong to 33,650 dong/share; MBBank (MBB) fell 150 dong to 19,700 dong/share. Vietcombank (VCB) lost 700 dong, closing at 56,200 dong/share; VietinBank (CTG) fell 600 dong to 30,000 dong/share. VPBank (VPB) fell 500 dong to 24,000 dong/share. SSB andSHB fell 200 dong and 100 dong/share respectively.
Notably, foreign investors sold millions of shares in several banks, includingACB , BID, CTG, HDB, SHB, and VCB, putting further pressure on price movements.
Meanwhile, some stocks in the consumer, retail, and securities sectors, such as MSN, MWG, SSI, and TCX, increased in price. This development shows a divergence between sectors in the market, but there is not enough basis to conclude that the interest rate reduction is the direct cause of these stock price increases.
These developments occurred after the State Bank of Vietnam issued a document on October 18th, requiring credit institutions to adjust down deposit interest rates by at least 0.5 percentage points annually for maturities of 6 months or more; and simultaneously reduce lending interest rates, focusing on a reduction of 1.5-2% per year for manufacturing, business, and priority sectors.
At the meeting on October 19th, Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Pham Duc An reiterated the need for immediate interest rate reductions, while also urging banks to rebalance their profit plans and allocate resources to support both existing and new borrowers.
According to the Governor, the fact that banks are reporting high profits while businesses are still burdened with high interest rates could create the impression that the banking system is profiting from the difficulties faced by businesses.
You may also like
Bank profits face pressure, outlook is mixed.
In theory, lowering deposit interest rates helps reduce input costs, while lowering lending interest rates supports businesses in recovering production and operations. However, the problem is not simple when banks' cost of capital has just gone through a period of increase, while the economy's demand for credit continues to be high.
As of the end of last week, deposits increased by 11.22%, lower than the 11.44% increase in credit. This difference indicates that credit is growing faster than deposits, creating additional pressure on banks to balance their capital sources, while deposit mobilization remains challenging.
In addition, deposit interest rates increased significantly in 2026. According to data cited from SSI Research, by September, deposit interest rates at state-owned commercial banks reached approximately 8.3%/year; leading joint-stock commercial banks were at 8.8-9.4%/year, while some smaller banks offered rates of 9.8-10%/year.
If lending interest rates fall faster than funding costs, the net interest margin (NIM) will be under pressure. This is one of the factors that could slow down bank profit growth, especially for banks that have to compete fiercely to maintain deposit levels.
According to SSI Research, the overall NIM for the banking sector may slightly decrease by 2 basis points to 3.11% in 2027. Specifically, the NIM of state-owned commercial banks is expected to increase by 2 basis points, while that of joint-stock commercial banks is projected to decrease by 8 basis points.
Thien Viet Securities (TVS) also noted that bank stocks may experience stronger divergence. Credit growth remains a driving force supporting business results in 2026, but rising capital costs, difficulty in improving NIM, and bad debt risks could cause industry profits to slow down from 2027. Provisioning costs are likely to become more apparent in the 2027-2028 period, after a period of rapid credit growth.
Another issue is the potential for actual reductions in deposit interest rates. When listed interest rates are required to be adjusted downwards, banks may still face pressure to retain depositors through additional interest rate programs, gifts, certificates of deposit, or private agreements for large deposits. If these forms of promotion continue to be prevalent, the actual reduction in interest rates may not be uniform across banks and customer groups.
You may also like
Vietcombank Chairman Nguyen Thanh Tung stated that the biggest challenge facing the industry currently is reducing deposit interest rates. He affirmed that banks, especially state-owned commercial banks, are ready to reduce profits to support businesses; and emphasized that interest rate reductions need to be substantive, without accompanying administrative conditions or procedures.
The ability to meet this requirement is also affected by the macroeconomic environment. The CPI in September increased by 5.08% year-on-year, with an average increase of 4.52% over the first nine months, while high global oil prices increase the risk of inflation. If domestic interest rates fall while international interest rates remain high, exchange rate pressure could also return.
Regarding credit quality, the demand for lower interest rates does not mean lowering lending standards. Banks still need to control risks, assess collateral, classify loans, and make provisions as required by regulations. Therefore, small businesses and new customers without a good credit history or suitable collateral may face more difficulties in accessing capital.
On the positive side, if lower interest rates help businesses recover, improve cash flow and debt repayment capacity, the bank's asset quality could improve in the long term. However, this benefit takes time to be reflected in business results, while pressure on NIM and cost of capital may appear sooner.
Therefore, the outlook for bank stocks will depend heavily on each bank's ability to control funding costs, maintain stable capital sources, and ensure credit quality. Banks with advantages in current account deposits (CASA), low-cost funding, and strong risk management capabilities may withstand the challenges better. Conversely, banks heavily reliant on high-interest funding sources risk facing greater pressure on their profit margins in the coming period.

The next stage will depend on whether businesses can turn these established trade flows into new supply contracts, distribution networks and long-term investment projects. This article explains these development dynamics and is essential reading for anyone involved in Russian and ASEAN affairs.
The immediate Russian trade and investment opportunities are visible across Southeast Asia. Its 11 areas are trade and investment, digital transformation, science and technology, transport, agriculture, energy, mining, climate change, the circular economy, tourism and the creative economy. Businesses need workable customs procedures, reliable payments, clear technical requirements, transport links and commercially viable contracts. The Vietnam-EAEU Free Trade Agreement provides an existing route for tariff reductions and market access. The next commercial opportunity lies in moving from individual shipments towards processing, contract manufacturing, technology transfer, local distribution and longer-term purchasing arrangements.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has introduced a visa-free regime for Vietnamese citizens for one year, taking effect from October 15, 2026. The talks also explored collaboration with Indonesian satellite companies and state-owned enterprises, alongside Russian proposals to establish laboratories and educational programmes in Indonesia to provide students with practical training in satellite systems, AI and scientific research.

| Tân Phú Trung Industrial Park in HCM City's Củ Chi area, where a US$2.1 billion AI data centre is being developed to strengthen the city's digital infrastructure. — Photo courtesy of Tan Phu Trung Industrial Park | 
HCM CITY — HCM City attracted US$5.7 billion in domestic and foreign investment into its export processing and industrial zones during the first nine months of 2026.
The figure exceeded the city's full-year target by 31 per cent, highlighting strong momentum in high-quality industrial investment under Resolution No.10-NQ/TW.
Total investment reached 131 per cent of the 2026 target of $4.25 billion and represented a 29 per cent increase compared with the same period in 2025, according to the city's Export Processing and Industrial Zones Authority (HEPZA).
Trần Việt Hà, deputy head of HEPZA, said the inflows reflected a gradual shift towards projects with greater technological content, stronger industrial linkages and higher long-term value.
Rather than focusing solely on manufacturing capacity, many newly licensed projects are expected to strengthen industrial infrastructure, attract supporting industries and create opportunities for Vietnamese enterprises to participate more deeply in global supply chains.
Strong FDI growth
Foreign direct investment remained the main growth driver, reaching $4.3 billion, up 62 per cent year-on-year.
During the first nine months, HEPZA granted investment licences to 100 new projects with combined registered capital of $3.1 billion.
Another 120 existing projects received approval to increase their capital by a total of $1.1 billion.
Hà said the quality of investment was becoming increasingly important as HCM City pursues a greener, more technology-oriented industrial development model in line with national strategies for private-sector growth and innovation.
The largest project approved during the period is a $2.1 billion data centre in Tân Phú Trung Industrial Park.
Designed as high-performance computing infrastructure for artificial intelligence and large-scale data processing, the facility is expected to become one of the country's key digital infrastructure investments.
The project is also expected to stimulate demand across related sectors, including energy, telecommunications, cloud services and highly skilled technology employment.
Another significant development is Phase 1 of Vĩnh Lập Industrial Park, which has received investment approval from the city People's Committee.
The project covers more than 497 hectares with total investment exceeding $379 million.
Planned as a multi-sector industrial park, Vĩnh Lập will prioritise high-tech manufacturing while developing towards a green and circular industrial model in the coming years.
With annual investment targets already surpassed, HEPZA said its priority for the final quarter of 2026 will be accelerating approved projects, resolving implementation bottlenecks and promoting investment to strategic investors in high technology, research and development, innovation and advanced manufacturing.
High-tech momentum
The HCM City High-Tech Park (SHTP) also recorded robust investment during the first nine months of the year.
The investment trend aligns with Resolution No. 57-NQ/TW, which identifies science, technology, innovation and digital transformation as key drivers of Việt Nam's long-term economic growth, with priority given to strategic technologies, including artificial intelligence, semiconductors, big data and next-generation digital infrastructure.
The park granted investment certificates to four new projects with total registered capital of $1.2 billion, equivalent to 87.9 per cent of its annual target of $1.4 billion.
Among the new projects were two foreign-invested projects worth nearly $590 million and two domestic projects with combined investment of approximately $640 million.
In addition, five existing projects increased their capital by $57.5 million.
Nguyễn Kỳ Phùng, head of the SHTP Management Board, said the newly licensed projects were designed to complement the park's broader innovation ecosystem by strengthening digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing and high-value services.
The largest foreign-invested project is the Evolution Hyperscale Wholesale Data Centre, with registered capital of more than $508 million.
It is the biggest new FDI project approved by the park during the period and will expand the city's capacity in large-scale data infrastructure.
Another notable investment comes from Techtronic Tools Việt Nam, which will invest $81 million in a smart electronics manufacturing plant, reinforcing supplier networks and high-tech production within the park.
On the domestic side, the STARMASON hyperscale data centre complex will contribute around $480 million, while the Tâm Anh High-Tech Centre, with investment of $160 million, will expand biotechnology and advanced medical technology services.
Phùng said these projects would generate demand for high-quality human resources, technology services and closer collaboration between domestic and international enterprises, supporting the objectives of Resolution No. 57-NQ/TW and contributing to the development of HCM City's innovation ecosystem.

By the end of September 2026, the High-Tech Park hosted 165 valid investment projects with total registered capital of $13.9 billion.
Among them, 57 foreign-invested projects accounted for approximately 79.4 per cent of total registered capital, equivalent to around $11 billion.
The continued presence of global technology companies including Intel, Samsung, TTI, Nipro, Jabil and Nidec has strengthened the park's role as one of Việt Nam's leading high-tech manufacturing and innovation centres.
Looking ahead, the SHTP Management Board will continue reviewing land resources, upgrading infrastructure and preparing a new portfolio of investment projects.

articles.title: China’s economy grows 4.5% on robust exports as domestic weakness persists - Yahoo News Singapore
articles.summary: China’s economy grows 4.5% on robust exports as domestic weakness persists  Yahoo News Singapore
articles.full_text:
China said Monday its economy expanded 4.5% in the July-September quarter from a year earlier, driven by strong exports, a record that moves the country closer to its annual growth target just as trading partners press harder to narrow their deficits with Beijing.
The official figure beat expectations and picked up from 4.3% in April-June, the slowest pace in more than three years.
Chinese leaders have set a 2026 target of 4.5%-5%, down from last year's 5% expansion. Earlier this month, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) cut its forecast for China's growth this year to 4.5%, the bottom of Beijing's range.
Exports lift growth, but domestic demand stays weak
Exports remain one of the few bright spots. After a 36% jump in exports last month and a $938 billion surplus for January-September, China is on course to top last year's record $1.2 trillion trade surplus.
Higher US tariffs have dented bilateral trade, pushing Chinese exporters toward Southeast Asia, Latin America and Europe. High-tech goods, including semiconductors and hybrid and electric vehicles, are leading the growth.
In pursuing self-sufficiency to guard against Western export controls, China has built vast, heavily subsidised manufacturing capacity in sectors such as solar and EVs. But there have also been issues.
Output expanded quickly while consumption lagged, so much of it is sold abroad at competitive prices. Ecaterina Bigos, senior market strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management, said this tech-driven, export-reliant model has produced limited job creation and income gains, while the risk of AI-driven job losses is growing.
As such, the headline official growth figure is becoming "an increasingly poor indicator of how the broader economy is performing," according to Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board.
Zenglein believes, despite the impressive number, it hides "widening disparities across industries, regions, and households", and that managing domestic imbalances may prove harder for Beijing than handling outside pressures.
Domestic demand has softened, weighed down by a years-long property slump that has eroded household wealth and pushed up savings.
EU presses China to rebalance trade
China shipped about 919,000 passenger vehicles overseas in September, driven by strong foreign demand for plug-in hybrids and all-electric models, according to data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers.
For the first nine months of 2026, exports topped 7.1 million passenger cars, a jump of more than 70% from the same period a year earlier.

articles.title: Attracting FDI in an era of investment uncertainty: The new context and Vietnam's choices. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Attracting FDI in an era of investment uncertainty: The new context and Vietnam's choices.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
International landscape: fragmented, uncertain, and expensive.
 Geopolitics is becoming the biggest variable in investment decisions. 76% of investment promotion agencies in the 2026 UNCTAD survey considered tensions and conflicts to be the biggest factor impacting FDI, surpassing growth slowdown (58%) and trade uncertainty (54%). Middle East conflicts in 2026 increased transportation and insurance costs, pushed inflation back up, and led to the postponement or cancellation of many projects.
 Furthermore, trade policies, tariffs, rules of origin, anti-transshipment measures, and technology export controls are becoming part of the destination cost.
 High interest rates and rising bond yields are narrowing the capital needed for increasing infrastructure investment. 
 Another structural shift is the return of industrial policy, on an unprecedented scale, linked to economic security. Major economies use subsidies, investment screening, and localization requirements to draw capital to strategic industries, putting developing countries at a competitive disadvantage.
 For Vietnam, this is both a challenge and an opportunity, because what investors prioritize – macroeconomic and political stability, compliance credibility, clean energy, and skilled technical personnel – can be built through policy, not necessarily through government funding.
 Four major trends in foreign investment
 Firstly, the recovery is fragile and concentrated. Global FDI is projected to increase by 6% in 2025, reaching $1.6 trillion, but if transit flows are excluded, the increase is only 4%. Capital inflows to developed countries are expected to increase by 11%, while those to developing countries will only increase by 2%. The North-North corridor remains the dominant investment route, accounting for two-thirds of total capital and growing fastest when transit flows are excluded: a 32.2% increase between 2018 and 2024. Developing countries are significantly increasing their outbound investment (115% if China is excluded), but South-South investment without transit flows is only increasing by 19.6%, while South-North investment is increasing by 31%. Chinese capital in Southern countries (without transit flows) is increasing by 113%. G7 capital in developing countries outside of China is increasing by 31.5%, faster than in China (9.1%), showing signs of a "China + 1" trend. Vietnam therefore needs to attract shifting capital flows, but also needs to manage Southern capital and transit capital well so as not to become a "transit point". Investment from developing countries to developed countries to access technology is a major trend. 
 In a high-interest rate environment, foreign borrowing is very expensive, and the banking system is already under heavy strain (loan-to-deposit ratio around 115%). FDI is long-term capital, does not create debt, and generates net foreign exchange. Attracting high-quality FDI is therefore also a component of a strategy to finance growth and stabilize the balance of payments.  Secondly, capital is flowing into strategic sectors in developed countries. New investment (greenfield) in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, data centers, semiconductors, essential minerals, and clean energy technologies increased from US$109 billion in 2020 to US$576 billion in 2025, with the share increasing from 16% to 44%; semiconductors are growing at an average rate of 54% per year. Vietnam has found its "entry point" in segments such as packaging, testing, and design; Amkor's US$4.5 billion project is among the top 10 largest projects in Asia in 2025.
 Third, traditional manufacturing is shrinking. In developing Asia, greenfield investment in manufacturing is projected to decrease by 28% in 2025, and in global value chain-intensive industries by 31%. In Southeast Asia alone, this sector is expected to decline from $31 billion to $14 billion. The "regionalization" hypothesis is not supported by data: semiconductors, AI, and batteries depend more on capabilities than geographical distance. The "China + 1" advantage does not automatically apply to Vietnam.
 Fourth, investors are becoming more diversified, particularly sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) and state-owned enterprises. Completed cross-border M&A transactions by SO-MNEs averaged $85 billion annually during the 2021-2025 period, compared to $45 billion in the 2015-2019 period. Pending transactions announced in 2025 could bring total state investment activity to around $160 billion, equivalent to about 10% of global FDI flows. The combination of traditional state-owned enterprises and private equity investors is making the global investor landscape more diversified, playing an increasingly important role in FDI flows.
 How are countries responding to this policy?
 In 2025, 104 countries enacted 229 investment policy measures, the highest number ever; 73% were favorable to investors, but the proportion of restrictive measures increased to 27%. There are five main approaches.
 Firstly, incentives are shifting towards a targeted and results-based approach. Malaysia only applies preferential tax rates in the Johor Special Economic Zone in Singapore to certain strategic sectors. Vietnam is also following this direction, with the 2025 Corporate Income Tax Law removing industrial zones as an independent basis for incentives and focusing the Investment Support Fund on R&D and training.
 Secondly, security screening is expanding. The number of economies with investment screening mechanisms has increased sharply, while the US and EU still control overseas investment in semiconductor, AI, and quantum fields.
 Third, localization. Approximately one-fifth of the restrictions require the use of local labor, suppliers, or ownership; Thailand requires projects with over 100 workers to maintain at least 70% Thai labor.
 Fourth, retain investors and maintain the destination's reputation in the face of protectionist trends through credit guarantee packages, time-limited support... and tightened origin checks and anti-transshipment measures.
 Fifth, conditional priorities and co-investment funds. Turkey (HAMLE program) selected 1,126 priority products using a publicly available quantitative method; Thailand used the Eastern Economic Corridor with a pilot mechanism; Malaysia allocated $5.3 billion to train 60,000 semiconductor engineers...
 Some recommendations
 The scale of FDI into Vietnam currently ranks third in Southeast Asia, after Singapore – a regional financial center – and on par with Indonesia. In 2026, capital flows are expected to improve significantly: in the first eight months of the year, registered capital reached US$40.6 billion (a 55.4% increase), and disbursed capital reached US$17.25 billion (a 12% increase, the highest in five years). However, Vietnam also needs to focus on the following solutions to achieve its FDI strategic goals:
 First, shift from "attracting many" to "positioning correctly." A strategy to attract large global corporations requires a quantitative, transparent methodology like HAMLE to select specific segments where Vietnam can succeed within five years: for semiconductors, this includes packaging, advanced testing, design, and materials; for AI, it's data centers linked to clean energy. The portfolio should be updated annually, linked to specific projects, target investors, and responsible parties.
 Second, results-based incentives, compatible with global minimum tax rates. Applying a "commit - measure - pay" model: support based on actual costs for R&D, training, and supplier development; payments upon achievement of localization targets, number of Vietnamese engineers trained, and value of purchases from small and medium-sized enterprises; and transparent annual evaluations.
 Third, compete based on fundamental capabilities instead of subsidies. Focus budget on stable clean energy with predictable prices (expanding direct power trading), clean land, shared laboratories, controlled testing mechanisms, and especially training semiconductor and AI engineers to co-design with FDI enterprises.
 Fourth, transform FDI into a driving force for domestic businesses. Establish FDI-domestic business connection centers based on a supplier development model, where leading businesses commit to a certain number of Vietnamese suppliers meeting standards, and the State co-finances certification and digital transformation.
 Fifth, manage investment security proportionally. Avoid both mass industry bans and comprehensive screening beyond capacity: publicly list key entities and assets, integrate "warning points" into investment registration and share purchase procedures, establish processing deadlines and conditional approvals; review older generation investment agreements to reduce litigation risks.
 Six, protect the reputation of the destination. Continue to tighten origin regulations and combat transshipment; build a database of ultimate beneficiaries of FDI enterprises, especially those with capital transshipped through intermediaries; certify "compliant producers" so that legitimate businesses are not negatively affected.
 Seven, retain existing investors and mobilize co-investment capital. Establish a rapid response mechanism in case of shocks: regular dialogue with the largest investors, export credit guarantees, time-limited working capital support, conditional policy stability commitments for exceptionally large projects. Form a national investment platform linked to international financial centers to attract international funds into digital infrastructure, energy, and logistics.
 Eight, diversify partners along four corridors. Promote partnerships specifically with the US, Japan, South Korea, and the EU to attract G7 capital leaving China; differentiate between real capital and transit capital in the South-South corridor; support Vietnamese businesses investing abroad to access technology and markets.

Prime Minister Le Minh Hung emphasized that in the coming period, the government will resolutely cut down on intermediaries to reduce the prices of gasoline, medicines, and medical equipment. Land and real estate prices are also expected to decrease as the State strongly regulates them.
When inflation rises, the gains of economic growth will be eroded.
Continuing the agenda of the 2nd session of the 16th National Assembly, speaking in the group discussion this afternoon, October 18th, on the socio-economic situation, Prime Minister Le Minh Hung emphasized the great efforts in macroeconomic management to keep inflation at 4.52% over the past nine months.
Amidst sharply rising global oil prices, if tax measures are not implemented immediately, domestic fuel prices are expected to increase by approximately 60% - 80%. This increase in fuel prices will then impact the prices of many other goods; transportation, travel, and food will all see price increases.
PHOTO: TRONG HAI
"Countries are facing significant inflationary pressure, forcing them to raise central bank interest rates to control inflation. But we are still ensuring a sufficient supply of gasoline and diesel at the lowest prices compared to other countries in the region," the Prime Minister said.
According to the Prime Minister, this year is a year of boosting growth and investing in science and technology , with electricity demand reaching its highest level ever. For GDP to grow by 1%, electricity growth must be around 1.3-1.5%.

There were very difficult times, but we still ensured electricity supply and did not increase electricity prices, thereby tightly controlling the prices of other goods and ensuring inflation control.
"If inflation rises, the gains from economic growth will be eroded, and people will not benefit from those gains."
"The responsibility for high growth to fulfill socio-economic development tasks is correct, but it must be on a very stable foundation. In 2027, the goal is to continue to firmly uphold the foundation of macroeconomic stability. We will apply a comprehensive set of measures to ensure inflation control and maintain the major balances of the economy," the Prime Minister affirmed.
"We cannot allow surcharges and intermediaries to drive up fuel prices."
According to the Prime Minister, the Government is resolutely implementing the directives of the Central Committee and the National Assembly to reduce input costs for the economy.
In the real estate market, the implemented measures and policies focused on the strong development of social housing and rental housing. This immediately caused house prices, especially apartment prices, to trend downwards.
Regarding land prices, when the National Assembly considers and approves the amended Land Law, the State will strongly regulate and determine land prices. "Therefore, it is certain that land prices and real estate prices will decrease," the Prime Minister said.
The head of the government stated that, going forward, the petroleum market will also be controlled, and the decree will be amended to cut down on intermediaries in the petroleum business and reduce associated costs.

In addition, the electricity system and businesses in the electricity sector also need to be restructured in order to reduce intermediaries.
Regarding the pricing of medicines and medical equipment, the Prime Minister stated that recently, the Government has resolutely demanded that agencies combat violations and corruption, revealing the enormous intermediary costs involved. Ultimately, people have to pay high prices for medical equipment and medicines. This is unacceptable.
During this session, the Government will submit to the National Assembly amendments and additions to several related laws, resolutely cutting out intermediaries so that people can access medicines and medical equipment at reasonable costs.
