 Speaking at the National Assembly's group discussion session on socio- economic issues , budget, and public investment on the afternoon of October 18, Prime Minister Le Minh Hung stated that the Government is resolutely implementing the Central Committee's directive on reducing input costs for the economy.
 "We have implemented some very decisive policy measures such as strongly developing social housing and rental housing, and immediately the housing market, especially for apartments, must follow a downward trend. With the National Assembly considering and passing the amended Land Law, the State will strongly regulate land prices, so land and real estate prices will certainly decrease," the Prime Minister affirmed.
 Still related to prices, regarding gasoline and diesel prices, the head of the government said that the Decree will be amended soon to cut down on intermediaries in the gasoline and diesel business, ensuring a reduction in incurred costs.
 Fuel prices will, of course, fluctuate according to the market, but they must trend downwards. We cannot allow surcharges or intermediaries to drive fuel prices up like this, the Prime Minister stated clearly.
 Regarding the prices of medicines and medical equipment for patients, the Prime Minister informed that the Government has recently resolutely demanded that relevant agencies combat violations and corruption. This has revealed the enormous intermediary costs, ultimately leading patients and the public to pay high prices for equipment and medicines, which, according to the head of the Government, is "unacceptable."
 This time, we will present to the National Assembly several amendments and additions to laws such as the Law on Medical Examination and Treatment, the Law on Pharmaceuticals, and we must resolutely cut out intermediaries so that people and patients can access medicines and medical equipment at reasonable costs, the Prime Minister said.
 The head of government also stated that the electricity system and businesses in the electricity sector must be restructured in the near future to create opportunities for price reductions.
 Similarly, in the agricultural sector, when violations regarding planting area codes and inspections are dealt with decisively, agricultural exports have increased significantly, especially durian. The Prime Minister further cited this example and affirmed the determination to implement measures to reduce input costs for the economy, thereby increasing efficiency, productivity, and value for the economy. That is the way to improve the productivity of the economy.
 Regarding macroeconomic management in general, according to the Prime Minister, without sensitive and timely management, it would be impossible to keep inflation at 4.52%.
 As an example, he stated that when world oil prices increased by 65% to nearly 90%, if we did not immediately implement tax measures, domestic oil prices could increase by 60%-80%. And when oil prices rise, it will impact the prices of other goods, causing them to increase as well.
 Many countries are under immense inflationary pressure and are forced to raise central bank interest rates to control inflation. However, we are still ensuring a sufficient supply of gasoline and diesel at prices that are among the lowest in the region. This results in a significant budget deficit, but to support the economy and the people, we must continue to implement these controls," the Prime Minister shared.
 Or take electricity prices, for example. In the context of unprecedentedly high electricity demand, and even during periods when it was very difficult to ensure sufficient electricity supply, we still managed to ensure electricity supply and control electricity prices from increasing.
 According to the Prime Minister, for GDP growth to reach 1%, electricity growth must be around 1.3 to 1.5%. The fact that electricity prices have not increased, thereby tightly controlling the price levels of other goods to ensure inflation is kept at 4.52%, is a significant effort in macroeconomic management, the Prime Minister emphasized.
 The Prime Minister acknowledged that if inflation rises, the achievements of economic growth will be eroded, and the people will not benefit from them. Therefore, the responsibility for high growth to fulfill socio-economic development tasks is correct, but it must be on a very stable foundation. “Over the past nine months, we have seen such results, and this is also the goal for next year: we must continue to firmly uphold macroeconomic stability. We will apply synchronized measures to ensure inflation is controlled and the major balances of the economy are maintained,” the Prime Minister said.
 Addressing another issue of interest to delegates, namely mobilizing resources for development, the Prime Minister stated that public investment is being calculated based on this year's double-digit growth. The capital needs are enormous, and the state budget can only meet a portion of them through public investment. Therefore, it is imperative that public investment is disbursed 100% and that projects are truly effective and have a ripple effect. “In the last term, we had approximately 5,000 public investment projects nationwide; this term, we must certainly reduce that by at least 30%. The Government has assigned the Ministry of Finance and local authorities and People's Councils to carefully review which projects should be prioritized for investment, because we cannot invest indiscriminately,” the Prime Minister said.
 Stating that the medium-term public investment program already has a list, some projects have been allocated capital, and some projects are still undergoing procedures, the Prime Minister said that the Government will allocate funds very soon in the end of the year and the beginning of next year, but the choice rests with the localities.
 "After allocating capital, you must responsibly choose which projects to invest in first — even within national target programs: projects that generate the fastest and highest socio-economic benefits, have a ripple effect, and directly benefit the people and businesses should be prioritized. This is a great responsibility of the localities," the Prime Minister emphasized.
 At the same time, according to the Prime Minister, the Government, ministries, sectors, and localities must mobilize resources through private investment, foreign investment, and other sources of capital in order to unlock the potential.
 Clearly stating that with a transparent institutional framework, a strengthened two-tiered local government apparatus, specific mechanisms and policies in various fields, and very specific programs and plans, it is necessary to focus on mobilizing resources. The Prime Minister requested that localities reform administrative procedures, reduce business conditions, and streamline internal procedures to create a competitive environment and attract domestic and foreign investors. Only then can we hope to achieve double-digit growth targets in the coming period, the Prime Minister told National Assembly deputies.

articles.title: 2026 Swiss-Viet Economic Forum ties poised for growth as EFTA trade deal opens new opportunities - vietnamnews.vn
articles.summary: 2026 Swiss-Viet Economic Forum ties poised for growth as EFTA trade deal opens new opportunities  vietnamnews.vn
articles.full_text:
| Swiss President Guy Parmelin delivers his speech at the forum. —VNS Photo Nguyễn Hằng | 
Nguyễn Hằng
HÀ NỘI — The business communities of Việt Nam and Switzerland are among the strongest pillars of bilateral relations, Swiss President Guy Parmelin said at the opening ceremony of the Swiss-Viet Economic Forum 2026 in Hà Nội on Sunday.
Swiss companies have been active in Việt Nam for decades, he said, contributing to industrial development, technological upgrading, skills transfer and job creation.
At the same time, Vietnamese companies are becoming increasingly visible and competitive internationally, creating new opportunities for partnerships and investment.
“Their success demonstrates that cooperation between our two economies is not merely possible, it is mutually beneficial,” the president said.
Bilateral trade has expanded significantly over the years. In 2025, trade between the two countries rose by nearly 20 per cent year on year to almost CHF2.9 billion (US$3.5 billion).
Swiss foreign direct investment in Việt Nam reached approximately $1.8 billion in 2024, up 14 per cent from the previous year.
“I am convinced that we have only begun to realise our full potential,” President Parmelin said.
There remains considerable scope to expand trade, investment and innovation partnerships, particularly in advanced manufacturing, life sciences and healthcare, sustainable infrastructure, clean technologies, digitalisation and innovation.
In these sectors, Swiss expertise and Vietnamese dynamism can complement one another, he added.
Speaking at the forum, Vietnamese Ambassador to Switzerland Châu Mai Anh said Switzerland’s expertise in specialised manufacturing, finance, healthcare and vocational education offered considerable potential for cooperation, while Việt Nam brought a dynamic business community, talented workers and openness to new technologies.
She outlined three priorities: strengthening partnerships between businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises; investing in skills and knowledge through cooperation among companies, universities and training institutions; and expanding sustainable development cooperation in energy, infrastructure, manufacturing and healthcare.
Silvan Wildhaber, President of economiesuisse said for Swiss companies, the newly-signed European Free Trade Association (EFTA) - Việt Nam Free Trade Agreement offers better market access, greater legal certainty and improved investment conditions. Vietnamese companies can benefit from deeper integration into global value chains, access to advanced technologies and partnerships with innovative Swiss businesses.
However, signing the agreement is only the beginning. Its success will depend on the practical opportunities it creates - helping Swiss SMEs export more easily, enabling Vietnamese suppliers to reach new customers, boosting investor confidence and fostering innovative partnerships.
Tangible results
| Minister of Industry and Trade Lê Mạnh Hùng speaks at the forum. — VNS Photo Nguyễn Hằng | 
Minister of Industry and Trade Lê Mạnh Hùng said the signing of the EFTA - Việt Nam FTA on the same day marked a major milestone in economic and trade relations between Việt Nam and the EFTA member states.
The agreement, concluded after 14 years of negotiations and 21 rounds of talks, demonstrated the strong political will and sustained efforts of both sides, he said, expressing his gratitude to President Parmelin and the negotiating delegations for their active and valuable contributions.
The gathering of the two business communities immediately after the signing ceremony sent a clear message: the agreement's true value would be measured by the cooperation opportunities realised and the tangible commercial results achieved.
He said the agreement provided a stable, transparent and predictable framework for cooperation amid global economic uncertainty, combining Việt Nam’s expanding manufacturing capabilities and international integration with Switzerland and other EFTA members’ strengths in advanced technology, innovation and finance.
He identified four priorities: developing manufacturing industries and supply chains; accelerating the energy transition and green growth; promoting innovation, the digital economy, healthcare and life sciences; and developing skilled workers, drawing on Switzerland’s dual vocational education and training model.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade would work with relevant agencies and businesses to turn these priorities into concrete programmes and investment projects, he said.
Hùng urged Swiss and EFTA companies to view Việt Nam as a long-term investment destination and manufacturing base, while encouraging Vietnamese businesses to improve technology, governance, international standards and product value.
The Vietnamese Government remained committed to institutional reform, improving the business climate and helping enterprises capitalise on the agreement’s opportunities.
“I firmly believe that the success of the Việt Nam–EFTA Agreement will not be measured merely by the number of tariff lines eliminated, but by the tangible projects realised, technologies transferred, supply chains established, and competitive capabilities enhanced,” he said.
Agreement to implementation
Swiss Ambassador to Việt Nam Thomas Gass said that after 14 years of negotiations, the real work of implementing the agreement was only just beginning.
While the agreement can cut tariffs and strengthen legal certainty, it cannot automatically help businesses find customers, secure financing, build partnerships or overcome practical obstacles.
Its success will depend on three factors: whether businesses can understand and apply the rules easily; whether they can access reliable partners and financing; and whether the agreement delivers not only higher trade but also better jobs, skills development, technology transfer and more sustainable production.
Organisations such as the Swiss-Viet Economic Forum, chambers of commerce and the two governments will play an important role in addressing these challenges.
The Swiss-Viet Economic Forum 2026 (SVEF 2026) is taking place in Hà Nội from October 18 to 20, co-organised with the Embassy of Switzerland in Việt Nam.
The forum brings together senior representatives from government, business, financial institutions, academia and international partner organisations from Việt Nam and Switzerland.
Held against the backdrop of the EFTA - Việt Nam FTA, the forum aims to explore new opportunities for trade, investment and value-chain connectivity between Việt Nam, Switzerland and the wider region.
Under the theme “From Bilateral Strength to Regional Impact: Advancing Switzerland–Việt Nam Partnerships in a Connected Global Economy”, SVEF 2026 seeks to usher in a new phase of economic cooperation between the two countries. — VNS

articles.title: Representative Nguyen Nhu So: FDI incentives must be exchanged for technology and production capacity. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Representative Nguyen Nhu So: FDI incentives must be exchanged for technology and production capacity.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Representative Nguyen Nhu So argued that FDI incentives must be linked to technology transfer, improving production capacity, and helping Vietnamese businesses participate more deeply in global value chains.
Continuing the 2nd Session of the 16th National Assembly, during the discussion in Group 7 (National Assembly delegations from Bac Ninh city and Lam Dong province) on the socio -economic situation, National Assembly delegate Nguyen Nhu So, from the Bac Ninh provincial delegation, reported that the economy in the first nine months of 2026 showed many positive signs: GDP increased by 9.01%, the industrial production index (IIP) increased by 12.3%, and import-export turnover reached a record 888 billion USD, an increase of 30.4%. The budget deficit and public debt remained within permissible limits.
However, the pressure behind these figures is considerable. To achieve the annual GDP target of 10% or more, the fourth quarter must grow by approximately 12.5%. The CPI in September increased by 5.08% year-on-year, higher than the target of around 4.5%.
According to the delegates, the issue is not just the scale of growth, budget revenue, or the total amount of investment capital mobilized, but more importantly, "the quality of resources, their ability to transform into productive capacity, and their effective contribution to long-term growth."
Despite significant revenue surplus, the revenue stream remains weak.
According to Report 918/BC-CP, budget revenue for the first nine months reached approximately 2,187 trillion VND, equivalent to 86.5% of the projected figure, an increase of 12.1%. The estimated revenue for the whole year 2026 is 3,055.7 trillion VND, exceeding the projected figure by 526.3 trillion VND (20.8%).
Based on the government 's explanatory statement, the representative pointed out that in the surplus revenue, production and business contributed 270.5 trillion VND, approximately 51.4%. The three groups of revenue from land use fees (166.2 trillion VND), crude oil (19.3 trillion VND), and dividends, profits, and state financial revenue (39.3 trillion VND) combined to 224.8 trillion VND, accounting for approximately 42.7%. In the budget estimate, revenue from housing and land also accounted for about 25% of domestic revenue.
According to delegate Nguyen Nhu So, the budget still depends significantly on land and temporary revenue sources, instead of being guaranteed by stable growth in production and business.
Therefore, the focus of the evaluation needs to shift from exceeding budget targets to the quality of revenue sources, the ability to sustain them in the medium term, and the efficiency of expenditures; at the same time, it is necessary to separate revenue sources related to projects and PPP contracts to clearly see the actual contribution of the manufacturing sector.
You may also like
Credit is increasing, but businesses are still short of capital.
By September 3, 2026, outstanding credit reached approximately VND 20.45 million billion, an increase of 9.98% compared to the end of 2025. However, the average lending interest rate for new transactions has risen to 9.12% per year, an increase of 1.03 percentage points; some corporate loans even reached 16-18% per year. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) still face difficulties accessing capital and land, while the ICOR (Incremental Capital-Output Ratio) remains high.
According to delegate Nguyen Nhu So, the bottleneck lies in the efficiency of capital allocation and access to capital, not in the scale of capital mobilization.
Therefore, monetary and credit policies need to focus on improving the mechanism for restructuring corporate finances, unlocking capital flows to the production and business sector, removing obstacles so that businesses can continue to borrow capital, and creating a mechanism for businesses to restructure both cash flow and debt obligations. The delegate proposed four directions for implementation.
Firstly, reform credit access conditions: simplify application procedures, connect tax data and electronic invoices; encourage banks to assess credit based on cash flow, orders, and output contracts instead of relying too heavily on collateral. When refusing a loan, banks need to clearly state the conditions that have not been met so that businesses can rectify them.
Secondly, a targeted credit guarantee mechanism needs to be established. Decree 34/2018/ND-CP on the Credit Guarantee Fund for Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises has not yet fulfilled its role as a "bridge." Many businesses with orders and markets are still excluded from capital due to a lack of collateral. The State needs to share some of the risk with banks, prioritizing processing, manufacturing, supporting industries, export production, and high-tech agriculture .
Thirdly, improve the mechanism for converting debt into equity or share capital for businesses that still have the capacity to recover.
Fourth, transform the stock market into a medium- and long-term capital channel. The market was upgraded to a secondary emerging market on September 21, 2026, but foreign investors sold net approximately VND 135,000 billion in 2025 and an additional VND 98,300 billion in the first nine months of 2026, resulting in a sharp decrease in liquidity. The delegate requested clarification of the roadmap to ensure that the upgrade becomes a tangible advantage in mobilizing long-term capital.
FDI incentives must create domestic production capacity.
Registered FDI capital reached over US$50.36 billion, an increase of 76.4%; implemented capital reached US$21.7 billion, the highest in 5 years. According to delegate Nguyen Nhu So, the question now is how to transform that capital flow into added value, technology, and competitiveness for the domestic economy.
Delegates suggested that incentives should no longer be an automatic advantage. FDI enterprises enjoying higher incentives must make specific commitments regarding the percentage of purchases from Vietnamese businesses, developing domestic suppliers, transferring technology, and training human resources. Each project should become an "ecosystem for the development of Vietnamese businesses."
You may also like
"We need to put an end to the mindset of 'rolling out the red carpet but remaining outside the value chain.' Vietnam does not lack attractiveness to attract FDI; what we need now is the quality of that capital flow. FDI policy in the new phase must aim for a clear goal: every dollar of state incentives must be exchanged for new production capacity, new technology, and the maturity of Vietnamese businesses, " said delegate Nguyen Nhu So.
Regarding agriculture, delegates argued that the bottleneck lies in the lack of sufficiently strong enterprises to lead millions of small-scale farming households. Delegates proposed upgrading new-style cooperatives into agricultural enterprises for farming communities: land use rights would be transparently valued and converted into shares; farmers would become shareholders and receive dividends.
In addition, greenhouses and automatic irrigation systems should be recognized as assets that can be valued, traded, and mortgaged to enable agricultural businesses to access capital.
"If this problem is not solved, Vietnamese agriculture will continue to fall into a paradox: millions of households are engaged in production but lack leading enterprises; there is much potential but a lack of capitalization of resources; and there are products but a lack of competitiveness in the international market," delegate Nguyen Nhu So expressed.
To promote green production, delegate Nguyen Nhu So proposed the urgent issuance of a mechanism to support a 2% interest rate for green projects, the application of ESG, the development of a carbon market, and prioritizing projects that simultaneously reduce production costs, mitigate climate risks, and increase productivity. The delegate emphasized: "To achieve rapid and sustainable growth, we must both generate growth and proactively protect the capacity to generate that growth."

articles.summary: Indonesian stocks plummet amid a crisis of confidence.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The Indonesian stock market is experiencing its worst sell-off in nearly three decades, as concerns about transparency and the risk of being excluded from international indices shake investor confidence.
The MSCI shock exposes long-standing shortcomings.
The Indonesian stock market continued its plunge on October 19th, with the Jakarta Composite index at one point falling more than 5%, after losing 11.6% in the previous week's trading session, its sharpest single-day decline since January 1998.
Indonesian stock indices have fallen by more than 40% since the beginning of the year, while the sell-off has spread to bond and currency markets, pushing the rupiah close to record lows against the US dollar.
The immediate cause is a warning from MSCI, the organization that provides stock market indices used by many international investment funds as a basis for capital allocation.
On October 15th, MSCI announced it was considering moving Indonesia from the emerging markets group to the independent markets group, instead of just downgrading it to the frontier markets group as previously warned.
This classification falls outside of MSCI's main investment market groups, potentially leading to Indonesian stocks being excluded from key international indices.
This warning is particularly serious for Indonesia, Southeast Asia's largest economy , with a GDP of approximately $1.5 trillion and maintaining emerging market status in the MSCI classification system since 1989.
However, large economies of scale have not been accompanied by commensurate improvements in ownership structure and transparency of the stock market.
In many listed companies, the majority of shares remain in the hands of founding families or large corporations, resulting in a relatively limited amount of freely tradable stock.
When the number of shares outstanding in the market is low, prices are prone to significant fluctuations, while large investors face difficulties in buying and selling substantial volumes.
Complex ownership structures and a lack of transparency also increase the risk of price manipulation, especially when transactions can be conducted between related groups of investors.
These are the issues MSCI warned about earlier this year, forcing Indonesia to implement a series of reforms.
Jakarta has announced a roadmap to raise the minimum free float ratio from 7.5% to 15%, enhance disclosure of information regarding shareholders owning more than 1% of a company's capital, and tighten supervision of unusual transactions.
You may also like
However, MSCI believes that these changes have not yet yielded sufficiently clear results across the market.
The organization even stated that moving Indonesia to the frontier market group does not fully reflect the severity of current shortcomings, particularly concerns about coordinated transactions and the effectiveness of handling violations.
Notably, on October 16, Indonesian financial regulators announced fines totaling approximately $117 million related to violations in the trading and allocation of shares by three companies, including those belonging to large conglomerates. Authorities asserted that this was the result of a prior investigation, not a hasty reaction to MSCI's warning.
While these incidents demonstrate increased oversight, they also highlight the risks associated with trading and owning stocks that international investors are concerned about.
Indonesian officials were surprised when MSCI proposed moving the market to the independent category, as previous discussions had mainly revolved around the risk of being relegated to the frontier market.
Some experts suggest that this stern warning may be MSCI's way of increasing pressure for reform, rather than signaling a decision that has already been made.
However, the strong market reaction also highlighted the gap between Jakarta's announced reform efforts and the level of confidence among international investors.
Pressure on international capital flows
The risk of downgrading comes at a time when Indonesia is facing numerous economic challenges.
President Prabowo Subianto's government implemented large-scale social welfare programs and public investments, while rising energy prices due to conflict in the Middle East added further pressure on the budget.
Investors are also concerned about the trend of expanding state role in the economy and the ability to maintain fiscal stability.
If Indonesia is removed from key international indices, many investment funds that build portfolios based on MSCI may have to sell shares to adjust their weightings, regardless of the business outlook of individual companies.
Goldman Sachs estimates that passive investment outflows from the market could reach $5.6 billion. Prior to this, foreign investors had already net sold approximately $5 billion worth of Indonesian stocks since the beginning of 2026.
The pressure from capital outflows is not limited to the stock market. As investors sell assets and move capital abroad, increased demand for foreign currency could cause the rupiah to continue weakening.
You may also like
A depreciating domestic currency reduces the profitability of foreign investors when converted to USD, which could further encourage capital outflows.
This development was partly reflected in the bond market, as the yield on 10-year Indonesian government bonds rose to nearly 7.5% on October 19, reflecting increasing pressure on the cost of raising capital.
If this situation persists, the government and businesses may have to borrow at higher interest rates, while the need for investment in infrastructure and production remains very high.
In response, the Indonesian Stock Exchange reduced the daily maximum price drop limit for individual stocks from 15% to 7% to limit volatility. Several large corporations also announced share buyback plans to support the market.
These measures may curb the immediate sell-off, but they are unlikely to address the underlying reasons for the loss of investor confidence.
MSCI is expected to make its final decision in June 2027, giving Indonesia more time to demonstrate the effectiveness of its reforms. However, the sell-off suggests that investors are not waiting for the official decision to be announced before adjusting their portfolios.

articles.summary: China's Q3 GDP growth set to pick up as exports power ahead, Money News  AsiaOne.com
articles.full_text:
BEIJING — China's economy likely sped up slightly in the third quarter from a more than three-year low, helped by hot demand for the country's technological goods and fresh policy support, but further stimulus may be needed to sustain the momentum.
Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as investment in AI-related sectors cools and trade tensions with the European Union escalate.
China's strategy of redirecting credit and resources from property towards high-tech industries has created a two-speed economy, where strong factory output and exports mask weak consumption and private investment.
Data due on Monday is expected to show gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.4 per cent year-on-year in July-September, quickening from 4.3 per cent in the second quarter — the weakest pace in more than three years, according to a Reuters poll.
The projected growth is below the 4.6 per cent forecast in a Reuters poll in July and would be below the lower end of the official full-year target of 4.5 per cent to five per cent.
"While growth remains near the lower end of the government's target range, recent data suggest economic momentum improved meaningfully toward the end of the quarter, supported by resilient exports, a recovery in manufacturing activity and the initial effects of policy easing," said Zhou Hao, chief economist at Guotai Junan International.
The official manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) showed factory activity rose in September, ending two straight months of contraction, while a private manufacturing PMI showed growth in activity hit a five-month high.
On a quarterly basis, the economy is forecast to have expanded 1.1 per cent in the third quarter, accelerating from 0.9 per cent in April-June, the poll showed.
China's exports power ahead
China's trade surplus widened more than expected in September as exports surged, keeping the country on track to surpass last year's record surplus of US$1.2 trillion (S$1.5 trillion) and likely intensifying trade tensions with major partners.
A deal with the EU to rein in Chinese hybrid-vehicle shipments could weigh on the booming auto trade.
GDP data is due on Monday at 0200 GMT. September activity data is expected to show industrial output growth accelerated to 5.5 per cent year-on-year from 5.2 per cent in August, while retail sales growth edged up to 0.6 per cent from 0.4 per cent. Fixed-asset investment in January-September is projected to have fallen 7.3 per cent, versus a 7.2 per cent drop in January-August.
GDP growth is forecast to edge up to 4.5 per cent in the fourth quarter, putting full-year growth at 4.5 per cent, before easing to 4.4 per cent in 2027, according to the poll.
In late September, Beijing rolled out a fresh round of support measures, including targeted interest-rate cuts and mortgage subsidies, after the cabinet pledged stronger action to shore up growth and meet its annual target.
Earlier this month, authorities also allocated 550 billion yuan (S$105 billion) in unused government debt quotas to help ease local government financial strains and support infrastructure spending.
"There remains room for further support measures, such as policies to boost employment and incomes and other measures to boost domestic demand," Lynn Song, ING's chief Greater China economist, said in a note. "Should economic momentum remain subdued into year-end, policymakers may respond with further fiscal stimulus and a broader easing of monetary policy."
China is likely to rely more on fiscal stimulus to spur growth, as faster producer price gains and a pickup in consumer inflation leave the central bank with limited room for high-profile monetary easing.
Analysts polled by Reuters expect the central bank to keep its benchmark lending rates, the loan prime rates, and banks' reserve requirement ratio unchanged through the first quarter of 2027.
An expected Politburo meeting and the annual Central Economic Work Conference in December could offer fresh clues on Beijing's policy priorities for next year.

articles.title: Commentary: Across the Yalu, China pours concrete over North Korean sanctions - CNA
articles.summary: Commentary: Across the Yalu, China pours concrete over North Korean sanctions  CNAWhat the New China-North Korea Bridge Really Means  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs MagazineChina keen to strengthen North Korea trade ties with New Yalu River Bridge opening  South China Morning PostNew bridge to open over China-DPRK border river  China DailyNorth Korea-China trade soared to $300M last month ahead of bridge opening: Data  NK News
articles.full_text:
A 12-year monument to mistrust, the China-North Korea bridge is open – locking in Beijing’s edge over Moscow and Washington, says this academic.
BOSTON, Massachusetts: For 12 years, the New Yalu River Bridge stood as the most expensive dead end in Northeast Asia. Completed by China in 2014 at a cost of US$350 million, the sleek four-lane cable-stayed span stretched across the border from Dandong only to terminate abruptly in unpaved North Korean farmland outside Sinuiju.
Now, after more than a decade of false starts, Beijing and Pyongyang officially opened the crossing to traffic on Oct 15.
Why open a 12-year-old bridge now? The answer goes well beyond border logistics. By turning on the tap of high-capacity commercial traffic, Beijing is physically retiring the era of sanctions-led pressure on North Korea – and ensuring that neither Moscow’s wartime courtship nor Washington’s appetite for fresh summiteering dilutes China’s position as the indispensable arbiter on the Korean Peninsula.
For a decade, the dormant bridge served as a barometer of quiet friction between the two socialist neighbours. After China finished the main span in 2014, disputes over who would pay for the North Korean customs complex and entry roads stalled the project.
Then came Pyongyang’s escalating nuclear tests, Beijing’s decision to back harsh United Nations Security Council sanctions in 2017, and finally Kim Jong-un’s draconian pandemic-era border closure. Opening a four-lane trade artery while the UN sanctions regime was at its peak would have been diplomatically awkward for Beijing and quarantined by Pyongyang.
That calculus has now inverted. Beijing has already dropped the word “denuclearisation” from its public diplomacy with Pyongyang, shifting from viewing North Korea’s nuclear arsenal as a proliferation liability to treating it as a durable buffer that ties down American military attention.
Once Beijing accepted a nuclear-armed North Korea as a baseline reality, keeping its primary commercial artery padlocked no longer made strategic sense.
The opening is the culmination of a methodical normalisation: cross-border truck freight resumed in 2023, the Beijing-Pyongyang passenger train restarted in March 2026 after a six-year suspension, and now the ageing single-lane Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge – built by Imperial Japan in 1937 – is being supplemented by a modern highway designed for heavy containerised freight.
THE RUSSIA CARD
Yet timing in Northeast Asia is never accidental, and two popular misreadings of this moment deserve to be challenged.
The first is the widespread notion that Kim Jong-un successfully used his high-profile military partnership with Vladimir Putin to strong-arm a reluctant China into re-engaging.
On the surface, the optics are seductive. Just five weeks ago, on Sep 7, North Korea and Russia inaugurated their first road bridge across the Tumen River, a project that raced from groundbreaking in April 2025 to ribbon-cutting in roughly 16 months.
Compared with China’s 12-year delay on the Yalu, Moscow’s sprint looked like a triumph of wartime expediency.
But optics should not be confused with economic gravity. China still accounts for over 98 per cent of North Korea’s official external trade. That single figure remains the defining reality of Pyongyang’s external relations – regardless of how “deep and close” its booming alignment with Moscow may appear to outside observers.
Moscow can supply Pyongyang with immediate security assurances, fuel, grain, and battlefield technologies in exchange for munitions and troops. What Russia’s sparsely populated Far East cannot provide is the industrial supply chain, consumer goods, agricultural inputs, and commercial scale that keep the North Korean economy functioning.
The “Russia card” certainly gave Kim the breathing room to negotiate with Beijing from a position of confidence rather than desperation. In the end, though, geography and scale bring Pyongyang back to the Yalu. By opening the bridge five weeks after the Tumen crossing, Beijing is reminding both Pyongyang and the world where the Peninsula’s real economic lifeline lies.
Once Beijing accepted a nuclear-armed North Korea as a baseline reality, keeping its primary commercial artery padlocked no longer made strategic sense.
NO THREE-WAY MILITARY PACT
The second misconception is that twin bridge openings with Russia and China within five weeks prove that a formal, monolithic Beijing-Moscow-Pyongyang bloc has locked into place. In reality, Beijing is moving to protect its bilateral leverage precisely because its horizon differs from Moscow’s.
Russia and North Korea are currently bound by urgent, transactional wartime needs, making both capitals comfortable with visible geopolitical disruption. Beijing’s priorities are fundamentally different.
As a global trading power deeply integrated into international markets, China wants a stable buffer state in Pyongyang and a resilient partner in Moscow, but it prefers to manage its relations with both on separate bilateral tracks rather than appearing to endorse a formal trilateral axis that could invite secondary sanctions or harden allied counter-coalitions.
Revitalising Liaoning province – for which Dandong is the commercial gateway – and anchoring North Korea inside China’s economic orbit achieves Beijing’s goals without the diplomatic costs of a three-way military pact.
Finally, the bridge’s opening carries a stark message for Washington and Seoul. With US President Donald Trump having already acknowledged North Korea’s “57” nuclear weapons as a practical reality while hinting at a return to leader-level diplomacy, the traditional bargain of trading sanctions relief for denuclearisation is obsolete.
Physical infrastructure is destiny. A nuclear-armed North Korea connected by a four-lane highway to China’s industrial heartland and a new road link to Russia is insulated against economic coercion as never before.
If Washington returns to the negotiating table with Pyongyang, it will find that the economic leverage it once hoped to trade away has already been paved over across the Yalu.
Seong-Hyon Lee, PhD, is a senior fellow at the George HW Bush Foundation for US-China Relations and an associate-in-research at the Harvard University Asia Centre. This commentary first appeared on Lowy Institute’s blog, The Interpreter.

The deal, between Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) eliminates or reduces customs duties, including on imports of industrial, fish and agricultural products.
HANOI: Vietnam and four European nations outside the European Union (EU) signed a free trade agreement in Hanoi on Sunday (Oct 18), seeking to diversify their markets as United States tariffs disrupt global commerce.
The deal, between Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which includes Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland, eliminates or reduces customs duties, including on imports of industrial, fish and agricultural products.
The deal was signed in the capital in the presence of Vietnam's top leader To Lam and representatives of EFTA governments.
Vietnam said the agreement showed the parties' resolve to "reinforce the rules-based trading system amid continued volatility in the global economy", according to a government statement.
It was also expected to help Vietnam "diversify its import and export markets" and "integrate more deeply into global value chains", the government said.
Vietnam and EFTA concluded negotiations in July, more than a decade after the free trade talks officially began in 2012.
The parties relaunched negotiations in September last year, after they had stalled since 2018.
The agreement followed a global trade-disrupting tariff blitz by the US under President Donald Trump which has left Vietnam with a hefty tax on its US exports amid ongoing negotiations with Washington.
Experts say the new deal reflected a shared initiative to diversify commercial ties and reduce reliance on major trading partners.
"As the US increasingly exerts trade pressure on European countries, the agreement is a joint effort to turn economic integration into greater strategic autonomy and to develop alternative commercial relationships rather than relying exclusively on their largest partners," history and politics scholar Do Dinh Lam Khang told AFP.
For Vietnam, closer ties with EFTA economies could support its ambition to move into higher-value-added activities, Khang added.
The agreement covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, trade remedies and sustainable development, among other areas, both parties say.
Bilateral trade between the EFTA and Vietnam last year was valued at 4.8 billion euros (US$5.4 billion), according to the association.
Electrical and mechanical machinery, fish and pharmaceutical products were the EFTA nations' top exports to Vietnam last year.
Machinery, footwear and apparel were manufacturing hub Vietnam's major exports to the EFTA.
The association was created as a counterpart to the European Economic Community, precursor of the European Union which its four member states are close to but have not joined.

articles.title: Commentary: ASEAN’s quiet work before the next deadly disaster - CNA
articles.summary: Commentary: ASEAN’s quiet work before the next deadly disaster  CNA
articles.full_text:
ASEAN often gets criticised for the political crises it cannot resolve. The work it puts into preparing for major disasters is less visible, say Lim Junli and Ian Li from the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies.
SINGAPORE: An earthquake and a volcanic eruption simultaneously occurring, then a tsunami. That is not the set-up to a new disaster film, but the hypothetical scenario faced by the militaries of 19 countries in a September field training exercise. Held in Banten, Indonesia, Exercise Trident Resolve (XTR) took place just 40km away from Mount Anak Krakatau which erupted three weeks earlier.
And while the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) has at times been criticised for its ineffectiveness in resolving regional political crises, such exercises demonstrate that ASEAN has the ability to mobilise resources and international partners for humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR), if called upon.
Disasters respect no borders. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, one of the most significant disasters triggered by a natural hazard to hit the region, directly impacted at least 14 countries and claimed the lives of over 200,000 people from 38 countries. More recently, the floods at the Nepal-Tibet border affected citizens from at least 34 countries.
More than 40 per cent of global disasters triggered by natural hazards occur within the Asia-Pacific. As extreme weather events become more frequent and destructive, these will be one of the most pertinent threats to Southeast Asia.
The region’s densely populated coastal areas are expected to grow in the coming years. As climate change outpaces capacities to adapt and mitigate, the human cost in the event of a future disaster will likely be extremely high – not only in significant harm to life and property, but also the inevitable displacement of large segments of the affected population.
COUNTRIES CANNOT ALWAYS COPE ALONE
A major disaster can overwhelm any one country’s ability to respond, especially when those expected to help are themselves affected.
Following the Türkiye-Syria earthquakes in 2023, the needs on the ground were vast and immediate: Survivors needed urgent medical attention. Every minute counted in search and rescue efforts to locate those trapped in the rubble. Those displaced from their homes required emergency shelter, food, water and clothing, while more vulnerable groups such as pregnant women, children and the disabled needed special attention and supplies.
Efforts had to be undertaken simultaneously across at least 10 cities. Based on known fault lines, preparation had only been made with a smaller geographical area of damage, with neighbouring municipalities and provinces expected to contribute to emergency assistance.
But the unanticipated scale of the earthquake meant that those expected to help ended up needing help instead.
MORE HELP ONLY WORKS IF COORDINATED
When devastation far exceeds domestic capacity, international assistance becomes crucial. But more is not enough unless everybody can work together effectively.
Military assistance is often required to scale up relief operations swiftly. However, coordinating multilateral military assistance comes with its challenges.
Inherent differences in practices, hardware and culture between militaries may affect interoperability, making the whole less than the sum of its parts.
For example, militaries might not share the same standard operating procedures and terminology for the reporting of information. Their communications equipment might also be plugged into different channels. All these and any language barrier would hinder the flow of information.
And if an efficient and meaningful response to a large-scale disaster requires civil-military cooperation at the local, national and international levels, it must be prepared and practised well before it is called upon. Relevant parties must build collective capacity, develop operational experience, and strengthen trust and understanding.
This is what ASEAN and its partners practise through exercises like XTR.
XTR was distinguished by the establishment of the Multinational Coordination Centre (MNCC), led by Indonesia and supported by the Changi Regional HADR Coordination Centre that is run by the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF).
The MNCC was the nerve-centre for the entire operation, where military responders shared information and coordinated planning. Liaison officers from all participating countries were on standby to ensure that requests for the deployment of their respective military assets received home approval in a timely manner.
The MNCC also worked in coordination with civilian entities such as the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UN OCHA). To fulfil its role of tying everything together into a single unified response, it made use of SAF’s OPERA communication tool and information-sharing platform.
So even though communities are likely to face widespread transport and communications disruptions, the MNCC can piece together a picture of what is happening on the ground, identify urgent needs and coordinate assistance accordingly.
ADAPTING COOPERATION TO NEW THREATS
While digital technology has helped to enhance disaster relief, it has also created new vulnerabilities. If coordination is the most important ingredient for achieving mission success in a complex operating environment, the systems that enable coordination must be protected.
This is why the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus' (ADMM-Plus) Expert Working Group (EWG) on Cyber Security was included in this inaugural iteration of XTR.
A potential breakdown mid-operation to the OPERA system would be catastrophic, leaving teams spread across a chaotic disaster zone isolated and essentially forced to work blind. So while some soldiers were out in the field, others were conducting daily cyber assessments to ensure that systems and networks are sufficiently hardened, especially in the case that there is a malicious cyber actor trying to cause further instability by disrupting the relief efforts.
Perhaps more crucially, significant efforts have been made to ensure cyber hygiene, and to sieve out mis- and dis-information. For example, AI-generated videos falsely depicted the scale and location of devastation following the earthquake in Myanmar in March 2025, making aid delivery more challenging when credible information was already perceived to be scarce.
One highly encouraging feature of XTR was that 19 countries participated, meaning that every member state of the ADMM-Plus including China, Russia and the United States took part despite broader geopolitical tensions.
ASEAN’s reputation as a neutral convener allowed it to bring together disparate actors, even those with trust deficits. At a time when multilateral cooperation is called into question, initiatives like XTR lay the quiet groundwork to help Southeast Asians when the need arises.
Lim Junli is a Research Fellow with the Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief Programme and Ian Li is a Research Fellow with the Military Studies Programme. Both programmes are part of the Institute of Defence and Strategic Studies (IDSS) at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), Nanyang Technological University, Singapore.

articles.title: China’s Trade Surplus Nears $1 Trillion as Exports Surge - Global Trade Magazine
articles.summary: China’s Trade Surplus Nears $1 Trillion as Exports Surge  Global Trade Magazine
articles.full_text:
October 19th, 2026 | Written by IndexBox
China’s Trade Surplus Nears $1 Trillion as Exports Surge
During the January-September period, China’s overseas sales reached $3.37 trillion, marking a 21.3% gain compared with the same span a year earlier, ICIS reported. In September alone, inbound goods climbed 31.0% year on year to roughly $291 billion, outpacing August’s 28.2% increase to $282.4 billion, while nine-month imports amounted to $2.43 trillion, a 27.5% rise.
Read also: China Exports Surge 36.3% in September, Topping Forecasts
The monthly trade gap expanded to $133.53 billion in September from $119.1 billion in August, the widest in 20 months. The accumulated surplus for January through September came to $938.11 billion, positioning China to surpass the $1 trillion level sooner than it did a year earlier. In 2025, the country’s full-year trade surplus was $1.189 trillion, having cleared the $1 trillion barrier in November.
Technology Goods Fuel Trade Growth
Advanced technology items and transportation equipment have been key engines behind China’s export expansion in 2026, and inbound shipments have likewise been heavily weighted toward tech goods. Robust worldwide spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure has underpinned demand for Chinese technology exports and imports, including semiconductors and automatic data processing equipment.
Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at Dutch banking and financial information services provider ING, observed that as China climbs the value-added ladder, its most rapidly expanding exports increasingly feature higher-margin products, while lower-end manufacturing relocates to other parts of the region.
The geographic distribution of China’s trade has shifted as well, partly as a reaction to elevated trade barriers. Song pointed out that the US represented 10.3% of China’s exports during the first nine months of 2026, a steep decline from 19.2% in 2018, whereas ASEAN has emerged as China’s biggest export destination.
Shipments to the US jumped 39.6% year on year in September, lifting nine-month growth to 9.8%, as the trade truce between Washington and Beijing aided a rebound in bilateral commerce. That truce now runs through January 2027, and tariff reductions on $30 billion worth of goods such as toys, Christmas decorations and kitchenware are expected to sustain the recovery in Chinese exports to the US for the rest of the year, according to Song.
Chinese shipments to ASEAN climbed 52.3% year on year in September, pushing January-September growth to 28.7%. Exports to the EU grew 25.3% in September, the fastest pace in seven months, bringing nine-month growth to 16.4%. Shipments to South Korea soared 68.2% in September, the biggest rise since 2021, lifting January-September growth to 39.1%.
Song noted that the data breakdown indicates import growth stayed concentrated in technology products rather than signaling a broad recovery spanning multiple sectors.
Export Momentum Clashes With Soft Domestic Economy
China’s surging foreign trade stands in contrast to enduring softness in its home economy, where household spending and capital investment remain strained by an extended property-market slump.
On 13 October, the International Monetary Fund trimmed its 2026 China GDP growth projection by 0.1 percentage point to 4.5%, down from the 4.6% it forecast in July. The updated figure sits at the lower bound of Beijing’s official 4.5-5% target for the year. The IMF stated that weak household consumption and softening investment amid ongoing property-sector strains were only partially counterbalanced by strong export results. It anticipates growth easing further to 4.0% in 2027, with Beijing’s policy measures averting a sharper slowdown, and cautioned that elevated global oil prices, together with lingering uncertainty and structural obstacles, are likely to restrain activity.
Nomura characterized the economy’s present condition as a major divergence accompanied by domestic weakness. The firm observed that key economic indicators remained weak in August, while September purchasing managers indices showed only a seasonal uptick, and its economists anticipate just a modest growth rebound in September.
According to Nomura, net exports of goods and services are expected to add 1.2 percentage points to GDP growth in 2026, versus 1.4 percentage points in 2025, underscoring how much foreign demand matters in counterbalancing feeble domestic activity. Nomura forecasts a $1.161 trillion trade surplus for 2026, compared with the record $1.189 trillion in 2025, before the surplus expands to $1.272 trillion in 2027.
Export resilience may lessen the near-term imperative for forceful stimulus, though officials have already rolled out additional steps to shore up weak domestic activity. In late September, the People’s Bank of China, the Ministry of Finance and the National Financial Regulatory Administration introduced measures designed to reduce financing costs and boost central bank lending. These included a 25-basis-point cut to the pledged supplementary lending rate and a CNY 700 billion expansion of the central bank’s re-lending quota for designated sectors. Authorities also broadened pledged supplementary lending support to the government’s Six Networks infrastructure program and launched an interest subsidy scheme for mortgage payments.
Nomura said it anticipates only a modest lift from these easing steps. The firm expects Beijing to deliver further support but does not foresee additional cuts to banks’ reserve requirement ratio or policy interest rates during the rest of 2026, and its economists said Beijing is likely to keep fiscal spending proactive and monetary policy accommodative to tackle exceptionally feeble domestic demand.
Trade Frictions and Tech Cycle Present Risks
China’s growing trade surplus is intensifying pressure from key trading partners looking to correct widening imbalances. In September, China posted a $34.8 billion surplus with the EU and a $34.01 billion surplus with the US, the latter the largest in 20 months. On 12 October, the EU and China agreed to curb Chinese hybrid-vehicle shipments into the bloc, with specifics due to be announced in December.
According to Song, the recent US-China trade deal and headway in talks between Beijing and Brussels should foster a comparatively steady trading climate through the end of 2026, and he said key trade relationships appear set to stay stable through year-end, keeping this year’s main growth engine running.
Song warned that risks may intensify in 2027, especially should the global technology investment cycle lose momentum or new tariff actions emerge as China grows more dependent on foreign demand. Nomura separately flagged US-China relations, the pace of domestic policy support, property and stock market developments and Middle East tensions among the principal risks to China’s economic outlook.
A sharp deterioration in exports would eliminate one of the economy’s strongest pillars of support and heighten pressure on Beijing to strengthen domestic demand.

The Vietnamese government has proposed a target of at least 10% economic growth in 2027 to the National Assembly, the country's legislature, while pledging to maintain macroeconomic stability and keep inflation under control.
Prime Minister Le Minh Hung presented a report on the implementation of the 2026 socio-economic development plan and the proposed plan for 2027 at the opening of a National Assembly session on Saturday.
He emphasized that 2026 - the first year of implementing the 14th National Party Congress's Resolution - holds significant importance in establishing a foundation, building momentum, and generating impetus for a new phase of development.
The government aims for GDP per capita of $6,100, consumer price index (CPI) growth of around 4.5%, and average labor productivity growth of 8.6%. It also seeks to increase state budget revenue by 9.1% and significantly cut recurrent expenditure.
To mobilize capital, the government plans to diversify funding sources through bond issuance, ODA loans, credit, private-sector resources and increased investment by state-owned enterprises. It will also encourage FDI companies to reinvest their profits in the country.
The prime minister noted the government would continue to manage interest rates and exchange rates appropriately. He pledged decisive and effective measures to lower lending rates and direct credit towards production and business activities, exports, science and technology, and small and medium-sized enterprises.
The government will also accelerate restructuring and reform its development model to strengthen the economy's internal capacity, independence, autonomy and resilience.
It plans to develop a stronger domestic industrial ecosystem, prioritizing foundational and supporting industries, while establishing modern service and logistics hubs and special economic zones.
2026 economic performance
Reporting on the economic performance in 2026, the cabinet leader said 14 of the 15 socio-economic targets were expected to be met or exceeded. GDP grew 9.95% year-on-year in the third quarter and 9.01% in the first nine months, putting Vietnam among the fastest-growing economies in the region and globally.
Fiscal, monetary and other macroeconomic policies had been managed proactively and flexibly, he said. Full-year state budget revenue was estimated at VND3,060 trillion ($118.17 billion), up 14%, while tax and fee exemptions, reductions and deferrals totalled around VND360 trillion ($13.9 billion).
"However, these positive results do not mean that structural bottlenecks have been fundamentally resolved. There remains significant pressure regarding macroeconomic management, inflation control, and exchange rate stabilization.
"Deposit and lending interest rates stay high, even as the demand for investment capital rises. Small and medium-sized enterprises continue to face difficulties in accessing land and credit, while the structure of imports and exports remains not truly sustainable," he stressed.
The prime minister noted the State Bank of Vietnam had instructed credit institutions to agree on cutting lending rates by 1.5-2 percentage points for production and business activities and priority sectors.
Vietnam's stock market had received an upgrade in classification for the first time (from frontier to secondary emerging market by FTSE Russell on September 21, 2026), while Moody's had revised the country's credit outlook to "positive" from "stable".
"International organizations have highly rated Vietnam's resilience and growth prospects," the prime minister said.
According to the government report, industry and construction grew 11.21% in the first nine months, the fastest pace since 2015. Exports and imports rose 30.4% over the period, with full-year trade turnover projected at $1.11 trillion. This could mark the first time Vietnam's total trade turnover exceeds $1 trillion.
Total society's investment reached VND3,110 trillion ($120.1 billion) in the first nine months, up 15.1%. Public investment disbursement amounted to nearly VND643 trillion ($24.83 billion), equivalent to 63% of the year's plan and almost 13% higher than in the same period last year. Registered FDI reached $50.36 billion, up 76.4% and the highest level since 2021.
On infrastructure, Vietnam completed an additional 395 km of expressways, bringing the entire eastern section of the North-South Expressway into operation. The government also resolved a number of stalled projects that had faced prolonged delays.
For the remainder of the year, the prime minister said the government would "strive to achieve the highest possible results against its targets, particularly double-digit growth, while maintaining macroeconomic stability and controlling inflation".
It would introduce measures to lower lending rates and ensure adequate supplies of electricity and petroleum products, Hung said. "Localities must strive to achieve the highest possible growth rates, particularly the major growth centers," he added.
Parliament flags risks to growth outlook
Presenting the appraisal report, Phan Van Mai, Chairman of the National Assembly's Economic and Financial Committee, praised the decisive and flexible direction of the government and the prime minister, as well as the efforts of ministries, agencies and local authorities.
However, according to the committee, the target of achieving 10% or higher growth in 2027 reflects a strong commitment but presents significant challenges, given that the foundations for growth remain unstable, while inflationary pressures and the demand for capital and energy are on the rise.
The global economic landscape is projected to remain complex and unpredictable. Geopolitical competition, trade fragmentation, energy price volatility, public debt burdens, and high interest rates could heighten financial risks and narrow the policy space for many nations.
Notably, shocks originating as early as 2026 may continue to exert an impact into 2027. Sustained high energy prices or mounting inflationary pressures - potentially exacerbated by adjustments to tax and fee support measures - could make the task of economic management even more difficult.
The committee highlighted six issues requiring the government's attention in its future management and policymaking.
It said high economic growth was not yet underpinned by sufficiently solid foundations. The four localities with the largest economies - Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, Hai Phong and Dong Nai - accounted for nearly 47% of total gross regional domestic product (GRDP) and were all expected to miss their 2026 growth targets, according to the committee.
Private domestic investment had yet to make a major breakthrough, it said. Although it accounted for 53% of total society's investment, it grew by only 14%, the slowest rate among the three investment sectors (the other two are the state-owned sector and the FDI sector).
Exports rose 24.5%, while imports increased 36.7%, resulting in a trade deficit of $19.42 billion, the committee said. Exports remained heavily dependent on the FDI sector, while supporting industries, domestic content ratios and technological self-reliance remained limited.
The committee also noted that businesses and household enterprises continued to face difficulties accessing capital, while the recovery in purchasing power remained slow. They also had to adapt to digital transformation requirements and tax policy changes. These difficulties directly affected investment, employment, incomes and domestic demand, it stressed.
The National Assembly is expected to vote on a resolution on the 2027 socio-economic development plan on November 7.

articles.title: Malaysia is upping the appeal of technical trades, and its youths are taking heed - CNA
articles.summary: Malaysia is upping the appeal of technical trades, and its youths are taking heed  CNAEducators told to future-proof TVET  The StarHRD Corp approves RM37mil in training grants for Melaka  NST OnlineBudget 2027: RM8b TVET allocation to boost aviation, automotive sectors  The Malaysian ReserveBudget 2027 advances socioeconomic opportunities for Indian community, says PKR leader  The Sun Malaysia
articles.full_text:
Vocational and technical training is gaining ground in Malaysia among students and their parents. But companies need to play a bigger role – and salaries need a bump, say experts and those who have chosen that path.
SINGAPORE: After completing his Malaysian Certificate of Education (SPM), the equivalent of Singapore’s O Levels, Malaysian Nur Adham Syamsuzzaman opted for a technical and vocational path instead of going to university.
“I chose this route because I prefer practical, hands-on learning experiences as compared to memorising theories. I also don’t think I am academically inclined,” said the Johorean, 24.
Between 2020 and 2023, he obtained his Malaysian Skills Certificate (SKM) and got a diploma in welding. He began working as a welding inspector a year ago.
“My family was sceptical about it at first but became more receptive after they saw that I could build a career in the field,” said Nur Adham, who now lives in Selangor.
There were also opportunities for him to progress through upskilling and gain experience across different workplaces, he said.
More young Malaysians are taking the same path as Nur Adham as the country’s technical and vocational education and training (TVET) system takes steps to equip them for future-oriented fields such as artificial intelligence.
The number of new TVET entrants has increased by about 30 per cent from around 176,000 in 2023 to more than 230,000 in 2025, according to Azmir Mohd Yunus, head of the National TVET Council’s secretariat.
The total number of students enrolled in TVET institutions rose from about 400,000 students to nearly 460,000 over the same period.
The proportion of SPM and equivalent school leavers entering the TVET system also increased from 44 per cent in 2023 to 57 per cent in 2025.
The government is targeting a total TVET enrolment of 650,000 by the end of this year, said Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, who is chairman of the National TVET Council Committee.
"We are aiming for TVET to become the first choice for students, while recognising that academic pathways continue through public and private higher education institutions, with TVET focusing strongly on meeting the demands of the national labour market," Zahid told reporters on Jun 5 at a National TVET Day 2026 event.
That same month, Malaysia launched TVET 2.0 with a stronger focus on emerging fields like cryptology and renewable energy. TVET also covers more traditional fields ranging from automotive and electric work to culinary arts, hospitality, fashion and design.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said up to RM50 million (US$12.3 million) from the country’s High-Impact Programme fund, which is under the Skills Development Fund Corporation, could be used to strengthen TVET 2.0’s implementation.
Industry players said employers see an increasingly important role for technically trained workers in Malaysia. TVET training must become more responsive to what employers actually need, and offer students clear pathways to better-paying jobs and career progression, they said.
“Malaysia has made considerable progress in elevating TVET but the next stage must be about quality, relevance and industry ownership rather than simply increasing the number of programmes or graduates,” said Malaysian Employers Federation (MEF) president Syed Hussain Syed Husman.
FROM "SECOND CHOICE" TO FIRST?
In Malaysia, technical and vocational education have long been perceived as the “second choice” for students – as well as their parents – compared to going to university.
This is similar to some other countries including Singapore and the United States, where college degrees are seen as the path to white-collar jobs that typically pay more than blue-collar ones.
“Like many people, my family and friends regarded a traditional university degree as the safest route,” said Muhammad Faeez Abdul Halim, 30, a TVET graduate who got his diploma in precision machining at Penang Skills Development Centre (PSDC) in 2017.
“But I told them that there were good job opportunities in the industrial sector and that employers often prefer TVET graduates over university graduates for their practical skills,” he told CNA.
That perception has not entirely disappeared even as the government has sought to raise the prestige of TVET, experts said.
Arulkumar Singaraveloo, chief executive of human resource consultancy Malaysia HR Forum, said that while interest has grown, it has “not fully become a mainstream first choice”.
TVET has also yet to attract high-performing school leavers, he added, due to concerns over employment prospects, career progression and social recognition persisting among students and parents.
Malaysia has 1,996 TVET institutions nationwide, according to the government’s TVET portal. They include 897 public institutions, 44 under state governments and statutory bodies and 1,055 private institutions registered under the Department of Skills Development.
The institutions include vocational colleges, polytechnics, community colleges and skills training institutes.
But amid reports that some university graduates are also facing job insecurity as AI reshapes hiring and work processes, training providers said they are seeing signs of attitudes gradually shifting.
PSDC chief executive officer Hari Narayanan said it is receiving more enquiries about TVET from both school leavers and their parents, although the shift has not been dramatic.
“Most of the students are from the B40 category who want to learn but at the same time earn a living,” Narayanan said, referring to the bottom 40 per cent of households by income.
Penang-based training provider PSDC offers programmes where 70 per cent of training takes place within companies, allowing students to gain experience while receiving an allowance.
Universiti Kuala Lumpur British Malaysian Institute (UniKL-BMI) has observed a similar shift.
“Students are not simply looking for a qualification, they are looking at where that qualification can take them,” said the TVET provider based in Selangor, which also offers some technical education programmes across bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral levels.
Based on its observations, UniKL-BMI said that youths and their parents are considering factors such as employment prospects, professional certification, salary potential and industry exposure.
This makes technical pathways in areas such as semiconductors, electrical and electronics and digital technologies more attractive, it said.
Among employers, perceptions of TVET qualifications have “improved significantly” as companies face difficulties recruiting workers with the practical skills needed, said Syed Hussain of the employers federation.
“For many employers, a key consideration is no longer whether a candidate holds a university degree or TVET qualification, but whether the individual possesses the competencies required to perform the job effectively,” he said.
In fields such as manufacturing, electrical and electronics, mechatronics and automation, a TVET graduate could have a “distinct advantage” because of their hands-on training and exposure to workplace practices, Syed Hussain added.
The push for vocational training is also closely linked to Malaysia’s broader industrial ambitions.
The government has stepped up efforts on TVET in recent years, including through the establishment of the National TVET Council in 2020 to strengthen coordination.
Under Budget 2026, RM7.9 billion was allocated to TVET, up from RM7.5 billion the previous year.
Malaysia’s New Industrial Master Plan (NIMP) 2030 launched in September 2023 also identifies expanding TVET programmes for high-skilled jobs in critical sectors.
TalentCorp, an agency under Malaysia’s Ministry of Human Resources, identified 66 critical occupations where demand is high and vacancies are relatively difficult to fill, said Azmir of the National TVET Council.
They include industrial and production technicians, mechanical engineering technicians and welders, as well as data and cybersecurity professionals.
Under the National Semiconductor Strategy, Malaysia aims to train and upskill 60,000 highly skilled local engineers by 2030.
Malaysia’s “renewed emphasis” on technical and vocational education reflected an economic reality that the country has “reached the limits of a growth model built on low-cost labour”, said Kumaran Nair Shanmugam, head of vocational education and training at the Malaysian-German Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
“Malaysia has been an upper-middle income economy since the early 1990s yet it has not crossed into the high-income status, and closing that gap now depends on moving into higher-value industries,” he told CNA.
The availability of skilled local workers is one of the factors companies consider when deciding where to locate major investments, Kumaran said.
That is why ensuring a credible TVET system could improve Malaysia’s competitiveness, he added.
FROM A SUPPLY-DRIVEN TO INDUSTRY-DRIVEN TVET
Despite strengthened government support for TVET, observers and industry players said the system can be improved by being more industry-driven.
Malaysia’s current TVET model remains too supply-driven, said Wan Chang Da, a professor at the School of Education at Taylor’s University Malaysia.
It still “largely follows a higher education model”, where training institutions determine the programmes offered and their curricula, he said.
"Although (institutions) will say that there is industry input, the industry (players) are usually just taking an advisory role, not directly involved in the development of the students,” Wan said.
This differs from a demand-driven TVET, where industries and businesses are directly involved in recruiting students, determining the curriculum, training and, finally, hiring them.
The Malaysian Employers Federation agreed the country needs to move to an “industry demand-driven model”.
