articles.summary: Monetary policy maintains a stable pace, boosting economic growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Proactive response and market stability.
 Monetary policy management in 2026 will take place amidst a complex web of pressures. Geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East, trade tensions, and rising energy prices are impacting inflation, capital flows, and international financial markets. Domestically, the demand for capital to support production, business, and investment remains high, while the need for macroeconomic stability is increasingly important.
 According to statistics, as of October 15th, Brent crude oil prices reached $105.92 per barrel, a 74.1% increase compared to the end of 2025; the USD-Index increased by 3.8%. These fluctuations simultaneously put pressure on domestic prices, exchange rates, and capital costs. Therefore, every policy decision must consider the interplay between interest rates, liquidity, the foreign exchange market, and the ability to supply credit.
 In this context, the State Bank of Vietnam has maintained a proactive approach, coordinating various tools to meet the needs of the banking system while mitigating adverse external impacts. The focus of its operations has not only been on providing capital but also on ensuring the smooth flow of funds, contributing to market stability and supporting the activities of businesses and individuals. 
|  | 
| Managing monetary policy in 2026 will take place amidst a multitude of intertwined pressures. | 
 In the money market, the State Bank of Vietnam conducts daily repurchase agreements for securities through open market operations, with appropriate volumes and diverse maturities ranging from 7 to 91 days. This flexibility in maturities helps credit institutions proactively balance their capital sources, meet payment and disbursement needs, and limit liquidity pressure at any given time.
 Notably, the State Bank of Vietnam closely coordinates with the State Treasury in managing state funds to stabilize the domestic currency market. This coordination helps the regulatory body be more proactive in responding to fluctuations in budget cash flow, thereby supporting liquidity balance in the market.
 Along with open market operations, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) has flexibly implemented VND-USD swaps to supplement short-term liquidity support channels. Since the beginning of the year, the volume of VND liquidity support provided through this channel has reached over 336.5 trillion VND, equivalent to approximately 14 billion USD. This implementation simultaneously takes into account the requirement to maintain a reasonable VND-USD interest rate differential, supporting exchange rate stability.
 The State Bank of Vietnam also provided refinancing four times at the request of credit institutions, each time ranging from VND 15,000 to VND 25,000 billion, with an interest rate of 4.5% per year and a term of 2.5 to 4 months, to support agricultural and rural development loans. Through this, the central bank's support funds are linked to the credit needs of a crucial sector in the economy .
 With the coordinated use of various tools, the payment and disbursement needs of credit institutions are ensured to run smoothly; interbank interest rates tend to decrease. On October 14th, the average overnight interest rate was 3.58%/year, and the one-week rate was 4.34%/year. Liquidity is maintained, contributing to creating favorable conditions for the banking system to perform its function of supplying capital.
 In the foreign exchange market, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) manages the exchange rate flexibly, in accordance with domestic and international conditions, coordinating with interest rate tools, VND liquidity, and intervening in the market when necessary. As of October 16th, the central exchange rate increased by 2.05% compared to the end of 2025, while the interbank exchange rate was around 25,884 VND/USD, a decrease of 1.54%. According to SBV representatives, the market is operating smoothly, and legitimate foreign currency needs are being met fully and promptly.
 This result is significant for import-export businesses and investment activities. A stable foreign exchange market helps businesses be more proactive in payments, business planning, and risk management. Given the trade deficit of $19.42 billion in the first nine months, ensuring the supply of foreign currency for legitimate needs further highlights the need for closely monitoring market developments.
 Facilitate credit access and persistently support efforts to reduce capital costs.
 Along with maintaining market stability, monetary policy continues to focus on meeting the capital needs of the economy. As of October 14th, outstanding credit reached over 20.72 million billion VND, an increase of 11.44% compared to the end of 2025 and a 16.73% increase compared to the same period last year. This scale reflects the significant resources that the banking system provides for production, business, investment, and consumption.
 A key point in the management is that credit growth is placed in relation to inflation control and banking operational safety. The State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) projects credit growth in 2026 at approximately 15%, with adjustments made as needed to suit the actual situation. To support these growth drivers, the SBV is implementing solutions to create more room for credit allocation to important needs. Specifically, the regulatory body has a mechanism to supplement credit growth limits for commercial banks to provide funding to businesses implementing large-scale, key projects with spillover effects, linkages, and promoting regional and local economic development, as directed by the Government leadership.
 For real estate, the policy is designed to differentiate between types and purposes of capital use. Any additional outstanding debt compared to the end of 2025 for social housing, industrial parks, export processing zones, and certain types of tourism services will not be included in real estate debt when controlling credit growth in this sector.
 Alongside credit, interest rates are a key area of focus for the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV). The SBV maintains its policy interest rates, facilitating access to capital from the SBV for credit institutions; at the same time, it requires the public disclosure of lending interest rates, implements solutions to stabilize interest rate levels, and increases access to capital for businesses and individuals.
 Measures are being implemented continuously, from working directly with commercial banks to directing regional State Bank of Vietnam branches to inspect implementation in their respective areas. Coordination in refinancing, open market operations, and foreign exchange swaps also aims to support capital for the system, contributing to reducing pressure on market interest rates.
 As of October 10th, the average interest rate on new deposit transactions was 6.44% per annum, and the average interest rate on new loans was 9.07% per annum, both higher than at the end of the previous year. However, the State Bank of Vietnam's report noted that the overall rate of increase has slowed down over the months.
 At a recent meeting, Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang commended the State Bank of Vietnam and the Ministry of Finance for their close coordination in managing monetary and fiscal policies, contributing to controlling inflation, stabilizing the macroeconomy, ensuring the safety of the credit institution system, and supporting growth.
 As we enter the final months of 2026, the task of managing monetary policy and banking operations continues to present many intertwined challenges. The demand for capital to support production, business, consumption, and the disbursement of investment projects typically increases in the final months of the year, while inflationary pressures, exchange rates, and interest rates remain affected by the unpredictable fluctuations of the global economy.
 In light of this situation, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) has determined to continue closely monitoring domestic and international economic developments to proactively, flexibly, promptly, and effectively manage monetary policy; coordinating synchronously and closely with a reasonable and focused expansionary fiscal policy and other macroeconomic policies. The overarching goal is to control inflation, contribute to maintaining macroeconomic stability, support sustainable economic growth, and ensure the safety of the credit institution system. Operating tools such as open market operations, refinancing, interest rates, exchange rates, and credit will continue to be used flexibly and appropriately in accordance with market developments and policy objectives. Liquidity management needs to meet the reasonable capital needs of the banking system while maintaining the necessary conditions for the stability of the money and foreign exchange markets.
 One of the key tasks is to reduce interest rates, creating conditions for businesses and individuals to access capital at reasonable costs. The State Bank of Vietnam requires credit institutions to focus resources, reduce operating costs, share profits, and implement synchronized solutions to lower lending interest rates. This requirement is linked to the ability to balance capital, ensure liquidity and operational safety of each bank, and avoid unhealthy competition in capital mobilization that could destabilize the market.

articles.title: China is considering adjusting its policy interest rate. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: China is considering adjusting its policy interest rate.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
|  The People's Bank of China (PBoC). Photo: Reuters . | 
 According to Chinese financial news outlet Cailian , People's Bank of China (PBoC) Governor Pan Gongsheng said on October 19 that the central bank will study the possibility of shifting the key maturity of its open market operations to overnight at an appropriate time. In that case, the overnight reverse repurchase rate would become the key policy interest rate.
 This move aims to help the PBoC manage monetary policy more precisely. In fact, the overnight interbank lending rate has served as a target interest rate. Using this rate as the official benchmark will help the central bank's regulatory activities more closely track market developments.
 Following this news, the offshore yuan rose 0.1% to 6.6813 yuan/USD. Yields on 10-year and 30-year Chinese government bonds were at 1.64% and 2.06%, respectively; the 30-year yield fell by more than 1 basis point.
 Adjusting monetary policy
 The People's Bank of China (PBoC) introduced overnight reverse repurchase operations in June. Between June and September, the central bank conducted these operations monthly, with increasing frequency and scale. This tool helps to supplement liquidity in the banking system, especially at the end of the month or when tax payment demands increase.
 In October, overnight interbank lending rates fell below 1.3%, the lowest level since May. In June, the PBoC set the overnight reverse repurchase rate at 1.25%, while the 7-day rate was 1.4%, Bloomberg reported. 
|  | 
|  Governor of the People's Bank of China (PBoC), Pan Gongsheng. Photo: Reuters. | 
 According to analyst Wang Qing, the interest rate to be applied when switching to the new mechanism will be announced at the time of implementation. He noted that changing the key policy interest rate does not necessarily mean an interest rate cut.
 This plan reflects changes in China's financial structure. Bonds and stocks are increasingly becoming important sources of capital mobilization, surpassing bank credit in providing new capital to the economy . Meanwhile, lending is also gradually becoming less dependent on the real estate sector.
 Therefore, adjusting the policy interest rate is seen as part of the process of perfecting the monetary policy transmission mechanism, helping signals from the central bank to more accurately reflect conditions in the financial market.
 Furthermore, this change will help the PBoC control interest rates more precisely, while bringing China's monetary policy framework closer to international best practices. Central banks like the US Federal Reserve (Fed) have used the overnight interest rate as a key policy tool to guide yield levels in the bond market.
 "The current monetary policy framework is approaching international best practices, thereby facilitating the internationalization of the renminbi," said Zhou Hao, chief economist at Guotai Junan International.
 Expanding lending interest rate reforms
 Besides considering changes to the key maturities in open market operations, China is also aiming to diversify the mechanism for determining lending interest rates, rather than relying too heavily on the benchmark lending rate (LPR), according to Reuters.
 According to the aforementioned guidelines, financially sound businesses can choose a benchmark interest rate for floating-rate loans, based on the overnight reverse repurchase rate or LPR, after reaching an agreement with the lender.
 The PBoC also plans to expand eligibility for permanent lending facilities (SLFs) and develop liquidity support mechanisms for non-bank financial institutions, including insurance companies and fund management companies.
 These changes are taking place against the backdrop of improving economic conditions in China. The country's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 4.5% in the third quarter compared to the same period last year, exceeding analysts' forecasts. This result helps ease pressure on the 2026 annual growth target of 4.5-5%. 
|  | 
|  China's economic growth recovered in the third quarter, driven by export momentum, creating more room for policy maneuvering. Photo: Reuters. | 
 However, adjusting the key policy interest rate does not mean the PBoC will immediately ease monetary policy. According to Wang Qing, it is necessary to distinguish between changing the policy tools and deciding to adjust the overall interest rate level.
 Regarding exchange rates, Governor Phan Cong Thang affirmed that China has neither the need nor the intention to weaken the yuan to gain a trade advantage.
 The statement comes amid calls from several European countries for China to allow its currency to appreciate in order to narrow its trade surplus and curb record-high export levels.

articles.title: Developing high-end real estate based on market demand. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Developing high-end real estate based on market demand.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On the morning of October 19th, the National Assembly held group discussions on the revised Law on Auctioning Assets. Suggesting topics for discussion, Prime Minister Le Minh Hung emphasized that the ultimate goal must be to manage prices for social housing and rental housing. Regarding the high-end real estate segment for those with financial means, pricing will depend on market demand and requirements.
According to the head of government, the most important and ultimate goal is to manage and regulate land prices and the real estate market. This is a consistent objective in managing the real estate market and land and housing prices. For the high-end real estate segment, intended for those with financial means, development can be based on market demand and needs. However, the most important thing remains controlling the prices of social housing and rental housing.
PHOTO: DINH SON
Dr. Tran Viet Anh, Vice Rector in charge of Hung Vuong University in Ho Chi Minh City, agrees with the Prime Minister 's viewpoint. This approach is consistent with the principles of a market economy and clearly distinguishes between the roles of the State and the market in housing development. It is necessary to recognize the real estate market as a diverse market with many segments serving different customer groups with varying financial capabilities and needs; a single regulatory mechanism cannot be applied to all segments.
For high-end real estate, the State should allow the market to determine the product, selling price, and investment scale based on supply and demand. Businesses have the right to choose their investment segment, but at the same time, they must take responsibility for their business performance and the risks arising from their decisions. If supply exceeds actual demand, the market will self-regulate through selling prices, liquidity, and investment efficiency. Excessive state intervention in the product structure or selling price of the high-end segment is not only unnecessary but can also distort market signals, limit competition, and hinder the innovation of businesses.
You may also like
"Conversely, for social housing, housing for low-income earners and vulnerable groups, the State needs to play a proactive role in regulating and supporting it. Because housing is not just a commodity but is also linked to the right to housing, social security, and quality of life of the people. If this segment is completely left to market mechanisms, it will be very difficult to ensure access to housing for workers and low-income earners, especially in large cities and areas with a high concentration of workers," Dr. Tran Viet Anh commented.
Dr. Pham Viet Thuan, Director of the Institute of Resource and Environmental Economics, also supports the Prime Minister's viewpoint. He argues that the high-end housing segment is not merely a place to live, but also a powerful driving force for economic development, architecture, and national prestige. Luxury apartment projects, eco-villas, and real estate with global brands act as magnets, attracting foreign investors, billionaires, and experts to work and live there long-term. Furthermore, this segment meets the stringent living standards of the domestic super-rich, ensuring that large investment capital, instead of flowing abroad, is retained for reinvestment domestically. High-end towers often feature unique architecture, designed by world-renowned architects. They completely transform the appearance of major cities like Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi, rivaling Singapore , Hong Kong, and Shanghai.
The high-end segment consistently pioneers the application of smart technology, sustainable building materials, and green standards. This shapes a civilized lifestyle and elevates the level of urban management. The increasing number of world-class urban areas is the clearest evidence of economic growth, rising per capita income, and the booming purchasing power of the middle and upper classes. A country with high-end housing infrastructure and 5-6 star standard amenities will easily become a financial, tourism , and technology hub in the Asian region.
For businesses to compete, the market dictates.
However, Dr. Tran Viet Anh noted that letting the market decide does not mean loosening management. The State must still strictly control land planning and use, financial obligations, transaction transparency, and speculative and price manipulation activities. In particular, it is necessary to limit land hoarding, delayed project implementation, or inefficient use of land resources. Therefore, the State needs strong policies on land allocation, preferential credit, financial obligation exemptions and reductions, and simplified investment procedures to encourage businesses to develop social housing; at the same time, it needs a mechanism to control the beneficiaries correctly, prevent policy abuse, or turn social housing into a speculative product.
"Regulating the real estate market doesn't mean administrative intervention in every segment, but rather using the right tools, targeting the right people, and achieving the right goals. For the high-end segment, let businesses compete and let the market decide. For social housing, the State needs to create conditions for people to access housing at reasonable costs. Besides that, it's also necessary to focus on developing the commercial housing segment with prices suitable for the affordability of the majority of the population, especially the middle class and young people. This segment has very high demand but limited supply," emphasized Dr. Tran Viet Anh, adding that the State doesn't necessarily have to impose selling prices but should focus on removing bottlenecks in legal frameworks, planning, investment procedures, and land costs so that businesses can develop products at more reasonable prices. In the long term, a healthy real estate market is one with a diverse product structure, supply that matches actual demand, fair competition for businesses, and people having access to housing that suits their income.
"The most important principle in the Prime Minister's view is the need to respect market principles while not neglecting the State's responsibility to ensure social welfare. The market should do what it can, while the State should focus resources and policies on areas where the market cannot effectively and fairly resolve issues on its own. This is also the foundation for building a transparent and sustainable real estate market, creating momentum for business development while ensuring social welfare goals. The real estate market should not be managed with a leveling-off mindset," said Dr. Tran Viet Anh.
You may also like
Dr. Pham Viet Thuan also argued that the State plays the role of a facilitator, leader, and comprehensive controller to ensure that the supply of social housing reaches the right low-income groups; establishing mechanisms to control price ceilings and the standard profit margins of social housing developers to prevent collusion, price manipulation, or illegal transfers that undermine the social welfare aspect. At the same time, the State should minimize administrative procedures (licensing, approval of buyers), and provide exemptions and reductions in land use fees, VAT, and corporate income tax to attract reputable real estate developers. Furthermore, the State should maintain and expand preferential loan packages with stable low interest rates for 15-25 years for both ends, with the aim of supporting the basic social welfare of people and the workforce in large, highly industrialized cities.
Luxury real estate is a story of supply and demand and the competitiveness of businesses. Social housing, on the other hand, is a story of social welfare policies and the regulatory responsibility of the State. The State does not need to decide how much businesses must sell luxury housing for, but rather needs to create conditions for the market to have sufficient supply, transparent competition, and allocate policy resources to those who truly need housing support.
Dr. Tran Viet Anh , Vice Rector in charge of Hung Vuong University, Ho Chi Minh City

articles.title: Credit institutions share profits and reduce the cost of raising capital. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Credit institutions share profits and reduce the cost of raising capital.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
In his opening remarks, Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam, Pham Duc An, stated that the State Bank of Vietnam had issued Circular No. 9608/NHNN-CSTT last weekend on the implementation of operational solutions for credit institutions throughout the system, demonstrating a determination to achieve double-digit growth and prioritizing monetary security and system safety for credit institutions. According to the Governor, the banking system is considered the lifeblood of the economy . If the lifeblood is compromised, the body cannot be healthy. To achieve double-digit growth, maintaining a stable banking system and macroeconomic safety is extremely important.
The issue of reducing lending interest rates has received special attention and guidance from the Party and Government leaders, with the requirement to bring interest rates to a level more suitable for businesses and the economy.
Governor Pham Duc An emphasized: To effectively reduce lending interest rates, credit institutions must simultaneously cut operating costs, share profits, and reduce the cost of capital mobilization. Deposit interest rates are one of the most important components of the cost of capital; if banks continue to push deposit interest rates higher, it will be difficult to find a basis for reducing lending interest rates.
Interest rate reductions should not be applied indiscriminately but should be targeted, focusing on supporting priority sectors such as production and business. The policy of reducing interest rates should be considered for both existing loans and new loans, thereby helping operating businesses reduce their financial burden while supporting their capital needs for production and business.
In the first nine months of 2026, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) proactively and flexibly managed monetary policy to contribute to macroeconomic stability, inflation control, and economic growth. Specifically: It flexibly and proactively managed open market operations, aligning with market developments and monetary policy objectives; daily repurchase agreements for government securities with appropriate volumes and diverse maturities to support liquidity and stabilize the money market; managed exchange rates and the foreign exchange market in accordance with market conditions, absorbing shocks; coordinated various tools and monetary policies, and conducted foreign exchange sales to stabilize the foreign exchange market, macroeconomic stability, and inflation control; maintained interest rates at the current policy levels to facilitate access to low-cost capital from the SBV for credit institutions to support the economy; and directed credit institutions to implement measures to reduce interest rates. Credit management closely follows the directives of the Government and the Prime Minister , assigning credit growth targets with a 15% orientation for credit institutions to implement, with adjustments made to increase or decrease as appropriate to the actual situation.
Simultaneously, during the operational process, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) implemented solutions to create room for credit institutions to provide credit for certain important needs serving economic growth and to facilitate credit institutions in providing credit for certain types of real estate in accordance with the Party and State's policies; requiring credit institutions to strictly control credit activities in high-risk sectors and the real estate sector, directing credit flows into production and business sectors, priority sectors, and growth drivers, in line with risk management capacity, limiting the increase in bad debts, and ensuring operational safety. By October 14, 2026, outstanding credit to the economy reached VND 20,721,583 billion, an increase of 11.44% compared to the end of the previous year and an increase of 16.73% compared to the same period last year.
Recently, the international situation has been complex and unpredictable. Geopolitical tensions, especially the escalating conflict in the Middle East, have put significant pressure on international commodity and financial markets; oil prices have risen sharply, and supply chains have been disrupted. Central banks have reacted more cautiously to the risk of renewed inflation; some central banks have raised interest rates, such as: on September 16, the US Federal Reserve (FED) decided to raise interest rates by 0.25%, bringing the federal funds rate to the 3.75%-4.00% range; the European Central Bank (ECB) on September 10 decided to raise key interest rates by 0.25 percentage points - this is the second time the ECB has raised interest rates in 2026; the Bank of Japan (BOJ) on September 18 decided to raise its policy interest rate from 1% to 1.25%, the highest level in 31 years. High interest rates coupled with safe-haven demand have caused the US dollar to rebound strongly after a period of downward correction earlier in the year. These developments put pressure on monetary policy management in emerging and developing economies with high levels of openness, such as Vietnam, while the increasing domestic demand for capital to achieve economic growth targets poses numerous challenges to monetary policy management and banking operations.
At the meeting, commercial banks reached a high level of consensus and agreement on seriously and effectively implementing tasks and solutions to ensure system safety and contribute to the stability of the monetary market; strictly adhering to the regulations and directives of the Government, the Prime Minister, and the State Bank of Vietnam on interest rates; focusing all resources, reducing costs, sharing profits, and implementing comprehensive and decisive solutions to lower interest rates.
Specifically, they will adjust the listed deposit interest rate down by at least 0.
5%/year for terms of 6 months or more, absolutely avoiding aggressively increasing deposit interest rates, unhealthy competition, and causing instability to financial and monetary security; reduce lending interest rates to customers, focusing on a reduction of 1.
5-2%/year for production, business, and priority sectors; and implement solutions to ensure safe and effective credit growth, directing credit capital towards production, business, priority sectors, and economic growth drivers.
Providing credit related to the implementation of key, feasible projects serving socio-economic development and sectors that need to be encouraged as directed by the Government and the Prime Minister (science, technology, innovation, digital transformation , green transformation, digital economy, green economy, circular economy, education and training, cultural industry, etc.
); Strictly controlling credit granting activities for sectors with potential risks and for customers or groups of customers with large outstanding loans; Strengthening syndicated loans for large projects; absolutely not lowering credit granting standards or sacrificing credit quality to increase credit scale; Ensuring harmonious and balanced development between capital mobilization and credit, regularly reviewing the capital structure by currency and maturity, and diversifying mobilization channels; Enhancing management, operational, risk management, control, and internal audit capabilities; fostering strict adherence to legal regulations, discipline, and professional ethics in banking operations; complying with regulations on limits and safety ratios in operations.
.

In the coming period, the State Bank of Vietnam will continue to closely monitor developments in deposit and lending interest rates, and the publication of lending interest rates on banks' websites. It will implement appropriate monetary policy management solutions and be ready to provide liquidity support to commercial banks when necessary. The State Bank of Vietnam will strengthen inspection, examination, and supervision of banks' implementation of the Government's, Prime Minister's, and State Bank of Vietnam's policies and directives on deposit and lending interest rates; and strictly handle violations in the capital mobilization and credit granting activities of commercial banks.

Today (October 19), General Secretary and President To Lam, along with his wife and a high-level Vietnamese delegation, began a state visit to Denmark, an official visit to the European Union (EU), and Belgium.
Lasting until October 24th, the visit is expected to open up new opportunities for cooperation in enhancing development capacity and strategic autonomy, affirming Vietnam's pioneering role as ASEAN's gateway in cooperation with the EU.
Opening a "highway" to bring high-quality Vietnamese goods to Europe.
General Secretary and President To Lam's trip to Europe took place just one day after Vietnam and the member countries of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA, including Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway , and Switzerland) officially signed the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement (VEFTA) – marking Vietnam's 18th FTA. Witnessed by General Secretary and President To Lam, the signing ceremony was a significant milestone in the relationship between Vietnam and EFTA, which comprises world leaders in innovation, and demonstrated the determination of both sides to strengthen economic cooperation, promote free trade, and consolidate a rules-based trading system amidst a volatile global economy. Along with the Vietnam-EU Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), which has been in effect for six years, this new development shows that trade and investment relations between Vietnam and the EU are entering a new breakthrough cycle, creating a complete and interconnected economic space between Vietnam and the entire European economic bloc.
In fact, the EU continues to assert its position as one of Vietnam's top markets generating a significant trade surplus. Data from the Ministry of Industry and Trade and the Customs Department shows that in 2025, total bilateral trade reached over US$73.8 billion, with Vietnam's exports reaching US$56 billion. This growth is expected to accelerate in 2026. In the first eight months of 2026 alone, Vietnam's exports to the EU market reached US$44.26 billion, a 19.8% increase compared to the same period last year. Electronics, computers, components, textiles, and footwear continue to play a pivotal role. Notably, the most valuable aspect of the current export structure is not the production of raw or semi-processed industrial goods, but rather the strong shift towards high-value agricultural, forestry, and aquatic products. Vietnamese agricultural products such as coffee, cashews, frozen fruits and vegetables, and processed seafood are penetrating deeply into the retail distribution chains in Nordic and Western European countries. The tariff advantages from the EVFTA help Vietnamese goods maintain a "golden window" of advantage, gaining a head start of 3-5 years over competitors in the ASEAN region that do not yet have an FTA with the EU.
Conversely, Vietnam's role for the EU is also fundamentally changing from a low-cost manufacturing hub to an "economic anchor" and a strategic green manufacturing center in Asia. European investors now view Vietnam not only as a consumer market of 100 million people but also as a gateway to connect supply chains across the region. According to EuroCham's Business Confidence Index (BCI) report for Q2 2026, the level of satisfaction and long-term investment commitment of European businesses in Vietnam continues to remain high. FDI flows from the EU are clearly shifting from basic industries to high-tech projects, renewable energy, port infrastructure, and green logistics. Large corporations from Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands , and Germany are pouring billions of dollars into carbon-neutral manufacturing projects, offshore wind energy, and smart logistics centers to capitalize on the green transition trend.
Dr. Nguyen Van Dien, Head of the Department of Political Economy at the Regional Political Academy II, assessed that Vietnam is increasingly opening the way for goods to penetrate deeper into the European market – a high-standard, "expensive" but potentially lucrative market. Besides realizing new-generation FTAs, high-level visits by Party and State leaders also create important momentum, expanding bilateral relations and elevating trade connectivity.
Furthermore, another key factor in enhancing the position of Vietnamese goods is the domestic production capacity meeting international standards. For example, in the agricultural sector, our products not only comply with VietGAP standards but also meet GlobalGAP standards – a global certification standard. By successfully meeting stringent technical barriers, Vietnamese businesses are fully capable of conquering demanding markets, leading to higher commercial efficiency.
"Currently, many Vietnamese businesses, especially in the agricultural sector, hold significant competitive advantages in Europe. In the context of Europe being affected by geopolitical conflicts and fluctuating energy prices, leading to increased commodity costs, Vietnamese goods have even more room and opportunities to compete," Dr. Nguyen Van Dien commented.
Green economy cooperation and high-tech breakthroughs.
Denmark was the first destination on the working trip of General Secretary and President To Lam. Prior to that, on the first day of October, Pandora Group (Denmark) held a ceremony to officially inaugurate its factory in VSIP III Industrial Park (Binh Co Ward, Ho Chi Minh City). This is the group's first production facility in the region outside of Thailand. With an investment of $150 million, the factory is designed to achieve a capacity of up to 60 million products per year and create jobs for approximately 7,000 workers when fully operational. Ms. Berta de Pablos-Barbier, CEO of Pandora, affirmed that Vietnam was chosen due to its business environment, infrastructure, and especially its workforce with a tradition of jewelry making. The inauguration of this facility is not simply the opening of a new facility, but the laying of a foundation for Pandora's next decade.

This is Lego Group's sixth factory and the second largest in Asia, bringing tangible benefits to the local area and the entire country. The project is expected to create more than 4,000 jobs, especially providing opportunities for young workers to access modern skills and participate in the global value chain. This facility was built and designed to be the most environmentally sustainable Lego factory, utilizing renewable energy, while also contributing to Vietnam's commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050, as stated at COP26… As of the end of July 2026, Denmark had 179 active projects with a total registered capital of approximately US$2.5 billion, ranking 21st among 153 countries and territories investing in Vietnam. Many large Danish corporations such as Lego, Maersk, Vestas, Novo Nordisk, etc., have been developing their business operations and expanding their investments in Vietnam.
Notably, in addition to long-standing traditional trade activities with significant bilateral trade volume, cooperation in green transformation between the two countries is increasingly deepening and becoming a prominent feature of bilateral relations, especially since the establishment of a Comprehensive Partnership in September 2013 and a Green Strategic Partnership in November 2023.
Professor Vo Xuan Vinh, Director of the Institute for Business Research at the University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City, stated that European countries have successfully transitioned to clean and green energy. Therefore, through bilateral cooperation, Vietnam can learn from Denmark's experience in these areas, especially offshore wind power development – a field in which Vietnam is only just beginning. |  | 
| Market differentiation is becoming increasingly pronounced, requiring investors to prioritize leverage risk management over seeking short-term profits. | 
 In its recently published strategic analysis report, SGI Capital, an investment fund, has painted a multifaceted picture of the Vietnamese economy and stock market after the first three quarters of 2026. The economy is experiencing a strong recovery with GDP growth remaining high, aiming for double digits. Registered and disbursed FDI flows remain strong despite fluctuations from US tariff policies. Furthermore, industrial production and construction continue to be a solid foundation for growth not only this year but also extending into 2027.
 However, from the perspective of financial analysts, the macroeconomic euphoria cannot completely mask the underlying risks. Entering the fourth quarter, the Vietnamese stock market is facing two core challenges, requiring caution from both regulators and investors.
 Although monetary policy has been effective in maintaining relative stability in exchange rates and interbank interest rates, SGI Capital warns that this room for maneuver is shrinking. If inflation and international interest rates continue to escalate, balancing exchange rate stability, interest rate control, and high credit growth will be an extreme challenge.
 SGI Capital advises investors to carefully examine accounts receivable, provisioning ratios, and Group 2 debt during the Q3 financial reporting season, as these are early indicators of bad debt trends, especially for real estate loans.
 Overall, third-quarter profits across the market are projected to continue rising, but at a slower pace. Interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as real estate, securities, and banking may have reached their profit peaks, leaving the spotlight to sectors benefiting from commodity cycles like oil and gas, rubber, and sugar.
 However, the most immediate risk right now is the issue of liquidity and cash flow. Despite Vietnam's official upgrade to a secondary emerging market by FTSE, market liquidity has declined, falling below 15,000 billion VND per session. Foreign investors, after a brief period of net buying around the upgrade event, quickly reversed course and aggressively sold off their holdings.
 SGI Capital explains that the reason for foreign investors' withdrawal stems from concerns about inflation and rising global interest rates. Meanwhile, domestically, the supply of shares from new issuances is weighing heavily on the absorption capacity of domestic investors, while rising deposit interest rates are reducing the attractiveness of the stock market.
 Amidst a slowdown in new capital inflows, the historically high level of margin debt is seen as a ticking time bomb. Entering the fourth quarter, when the economy's need for cash surges to settle loans and investments, pressure to sell off assets (margin calls) could easily be triggered. Furthermore, the frozen liquidity in the real estate market is forcing many speculators to cross-sell securities to cover capital costs.
 In the face of unpredictable fluctuations, the top priority right now is not seeking profit at all costs, but managing leverage risk. Market differentiation is intense, and long-term opportunities are only truly available to those who can protect their purchasing power when market valuations are discounted to attractive levels.
 However, in the long term, the bottlenecks in the stock market are gradually being removed through drastic institutional reform efforts. The Ministry of Finance has just issued Circular 145/2026/TT-BTC (effective from November 16, 2026), creating a major turning point in trading infrastructure, especially the central counterparty (CCP) clearing mechanism and the regulation that does not require foreign institutional investors to have 100% of the funds before trading (NPF).
 Speaking with reporters, Mr. Han Huu Hau, CEO of Hy Maxpro, a specialist in stock market analysis, assessed: This is an important upgrade to the post-transaction infrastructure. The CCP mechanism and multilateral clearing not only improve operational efficiency but also help the market approach international practices.
 Mr. Hau emphasized that removing the 100% cash-to-value ratio (NPF) is crucial for unlocking foreign capital flows, giving international investors more flexibility in capital allocation. This is the long-term solution, creating a solid foundation for the Vietnamese stock market to truly transform and flourish in the post-upgrade era.

articles.title: The State Bank of Vietnam has requested a reduction in lending interest rates of 1.5–2% per year. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The State Bank of Vietnam has requested a reduction in lending interest rates of 1.5–2% per year.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) recently issued Document No. 9608/NHNN-CSTT on implementing operational solutions for credit institutions to contribute to macroeconomic stability, inflation control, economic growth promotion, and the safety of the banking system.
 Notably, the State Bank of Vietnam requires credit institutions to strictly implement directives on interest rates, focus resources, reduce costs, share profits, and simultaneously implement solutions to lower interest rates.
 For the time being, banks must adjust their listed deposit interest rates downwards by at least 0.5% per year for terms of 6 months or more; they must absolutely refrain from aggressively increasing deposit interest rates, engaging in unhealthy competition, and causing instability in financial and monetary security.
 Regarding lending activities, the State Bank of Vietnam requires a reduction in interest rates for customers, focusing on a reduction of 1.5-2% per year for manufacturing, business, and priority sectors.
 Alongside interest rate reductions, credit institutions must ensure safe and effective credit growth, directing capital flows into production, business, priority sectors, and drivers of economic growth.
 Credit funding should be prioritized for key, feasible projects and in sectors encouraged by the Government, such as science, technology, innovation, digital transformation , green transformation, digital economy, circular economy, education, and cultural industries.
 The State Bank of Vietnam also encouraged increased syndicated loans for large projects, but emphasized the absolute requirement not to lower credit granting standards or compromise credit quality for the sake of expanding lending scale.
 Banks must simultaneously balance deposits and loans, control liquidity risk, limit maturity mismatches, and increase the proportion of medium and long-term funding.
 Another important point in the document is the requirement for strict control over credit granting activities to sectors with potential risks, and to customers and customer groups with large outstanding debts.
 The State Bank of Vietnam requires banks to pay special attention to customer groups that show signs of involvement through managers, legal representatives, shareholders owning more than 5% of charter capital, collateral assets, investment projects, or common debt repayment sources.
 Credit risk assessment must be linked to real estate price trends, market liquidity, inventory levels in projects, and corporate bond issuance.
 Notably, the State Bank of Vietnam requires strict control over loans used for capital contributions, share purchases in unlisted enterprises, investment cooperation contracts in projects that do not meet business conditions, and loans intended to cover financial shortfalls that do not meet the prescribed conditions.
 The regulatory authority strictly prohibits the creation of credit profiles for the purpose of misappropriating funds, circumventing credit limits, and evading cash flow controls. Violations will be severely punished.
 For collateral assets, banks must value them accurately according to market prices, control revaluation that increases asset value, and regularly review the debt recovery potential when asset value decreases.
 The State Bank of Vietnam also requires close monitoring of Group 2 debts, bad debts, restructured debts, and debts with potential risks; proper debt classification, full provisioning, and accurate reflection of credit quality, without concealing bad debts or delaying risk recognition.
 Accrued interest, especially large, long-term, or difficult-to-recover amounts, must be strictly controlled. Dividend payments and profit distribution must ensure that business results accurately reflect the bank's operations.
 Specifically, the State Bank of Vietnam requires a comprehensive review of the entire portfolio of customers with large outstanding debts, as well as legal entities and individuals with potentially risky relationships, in order to proactively prevent and address potential issues.
 For banks that fail to comply with interest rate directives or engage in unfair competition, the State Bank of Vietnam warns that it will consider applying disciplinary measures between now and the end of 2026.
 In addition to legal action, the regulatory authority may review the credit growth target for the remainder of 2026, set a lower credit growth target for 2027, or require the application of higher safety ratios than those stipulated.
 The chairman of the board of directors, the board of members, the general director, and the control, audit, and supervisory departments at credit institutions are responsible for implementing directives and ensuring the safety and efficiency of banking operations.
